title: Festive Sales See Shoppers Log In But Hold Back On Big-Ticket Purchases
content: The festive season, usually a time to splurge, is telling a different story this year. A smaller number of card transactions and weaker smartphone sales are hinting at consumers tightening their purse strings amid mounting pressure on household budgets. Early data from Redseer estimated that India’s online festive sales clocked $7-8 Bn in gross merchandise value (GMV) during the first leg, from October 8 to 18. Nearly 100 Mn shoppers placed more than 350 Mn orders, with consumption running at around three times the everyday rate. However, the data also pointed to a more cautious spending environment. According to Datum Intelligence, a market intelligence and consumer data analytics company, the online festive sales amounted to ₹29,800-₹30,900 Cr this year, down 7-10% from ₹33,200 Cr during the corresponding four-day period last year. Card spending, too, declined 12-15% YoY. The broader consumer picture was also subdued. LocalCircles’ ‘Mood for the Consumer 2026’ survey estimated that urban households would spend ₹1.97 Lakh Cr on festive discretionary purchases this year, down 6% from ₹2.10 Lakh Cr in 2025. The survey received more than 67,000 responses from urban consumers across 307 districts. The trends pointed to a central challenge for retailers: consumers continued to browse and buy, but rising expenses, uncertainty over earnings and jobs, and less compelling discounts made them more cautious about committing to expensive purchases. Shoppers Tune In But Spending Remains Muted Flipkart’s ‘Big Billion Days’ sale, which opened on October 8 and closed on October 19, recorded 6.3 Mn concurrent users in a minute during its opening hour. Listed Meesho’s ‘Mega Blockbuster Sale’, which went live on October 9 and wrapped up on October 18, also reported a 75% YoY rise in day-one orders and 60% growth in transacting customers. Over at Amazon, the ecommerce major said that its nearly two-week long ‘Great Indian Festival’ sale (stretching between October 8 and October 20) saw the number of products ordered during the first twenty four hours more than double YoY. Redseer’s assessment also highlighted the expanding reach of online festive shopping beyond major cities. Tier II and smaller towns accounted for around two-thirds of shoppers during the first leg, while the number of first-time shoppers from these regions doubled in 2026. Gen Z made up more than 35-40% of festive shoppers, with demand across gaming devices, creator cameras,wearables, sports footwear, grooming and beauty. Around 60% of Flipkart’s festive demand came from non-metro customers, while more than 72% of Amazon’s visits came from outside the top nine metros. Meesho also reported strong growth in orders through its Meesho Mall offering. However, traffic, visitors and orders measured different aspects of shopping activity. They did not, by themselves, establish how much consumers spent or whether the average purchase value increased. Datum’s card payment data offered another view. On October 9, the first day Amazon and Flipkart opened their sales to all shoppers, card transactions stood at 83.5 Lakh against 82 Lakh on the corresponding day last year. Yet, the value of those payments fell 18% to ₹6,594 Cr from ₹8,067 Cr. The figures point to lower spending despite a similar number of card transactions. Meesho’s order growth, much of which came through cash on delivery, also illustrated why order counts alone could not establish the value of sales. The year-on-year comparison, however, comes with an important caveat. The major online sales in 2025 coincided with the September 22 GST rate cuts, which reduced prices on several consumer products. The opening of this year’s sales did not have a comparable tax-led trigger. Fashion And Select Categories Find Buyers Category-level disclosures showed that consumers spent on fashion and certain premium products, even as electronics faced pressure. A Bank of America research note (dated October 20) found that Myntra’s daily active users rose around 40% during the first six days of its ‘Big Fashion Festival’, which ran between October 8 and October 25, compared with its September average. Myntra’s monthly active users stood at around 93 Mn (up 8% YoY), while Nykaa Fashion’s monthl y active users grew 24% to around 17 Mn. Flipkart also reported a 42% YoY rise in beauty sales during the first hour of its sale, while its lifestyle category grew 12.5%, according to the company’s disclosures. Meesho also reported demand for festive décor and other lower-priced products. Redseer’s category-level estimates showed that large and small appliances recorded more than 20 times their average daily GMV during the festive period. Electronics ran over seven times the everyday level, while mobiles exceeded five times. These multiple compared festive daily GMV with the January – August 2026 daily average, rather than with the previous year. Amazon’s disclosures show that some premium categories performed well. Televisions measuring 55 inches and above accounted for 65% of its TV sales, while premium Android smartphones’ sales rose 70% YoY. The company also reported that high-end home theatre sold at 100X its regular day levels, while front-load washing machines with capacities of 9 kg and above sold at 80X. Fashion and beauty also recorded strong festive demand. Redseer estimated that fashion grew 20-25% and accounted for nearly a fifth of festive GMV, making it the second largest category. However, these numbers reflected performance in specific categories and do not establish a broad recovery in big ticket demand. LocalCircles’ survey provided another indication of household priorities. Among respondents who planned festive discretionary spending, 72% intended to buy clothing, footwear or accessories. Home appliances and furniture and travel and holidays were each cited by 45%. Only 22% planned to buy mobile phones, consumer electronics or gadgets. The findings suggested that expensive electronics were not a priority for most households planning festive purchases. Household Budget Under Pressure LocalCircles estimated that urban households would spend around ₹20,000 on festive discretionary purchases in 2026. While 57% of respondents said they intended to spend, 31% planned no discretionary festive purchases. The survey’s findings on how households planned to fund their purchases were equally telling. Around 83% of households intending to spend expected to use savings to some extent. About 34% expected savings to cover at least a quarter of their festive expenditure, including 16% who said they would fund the entire amount from savings. This came as retail inflation stood at 5.54% in September and food inflation at 7.74%, according to figures cited by LocalCircles. Higher everyday expenses left households with less room for purchases. LocalCircles founder Sachin Taparia said, “Household earnings are not rising, and inflation continues to rise.” He also pointed to concerns over AI and its potential effect on white-collar jobs, along with a lack of attractive deals on online commerce platforms. Discounts may also have done less to persuade shoppers to buy. The Economic Times reported that festive discounts were 35-40% lower than last year. The report also cited price increases of 30-40% for premium electronics in recent months. Smartphone Sales Exposed The Limits of Online Traffic Smartphones provided one of the clearest indications of the pressure on high-value purchases. Counterpoint Research’s early assessment found that smartphone sales fell 16% YoY during the first three days of Amazon’s and Flipkart’s festive sales, despite strong traffic on both platforms. The research firm had initially forecast a 12% decline in festive smartphone volumes. Its early assessment suggested that the fall could be steeper, although the figures available in the supporting documents did not establish the final full-season outcome. Counterpoint’s report identified higher device prices and fewer direct discounts as factors weighing on demand. Brands relied more on no-cost EMIs, bank cashback and exchange offers to make upgrades affordable without cutting listed prices sharply. Premium Samsung models, including the Galaxy S25 Ultra and the S25 FE, found buyers, but their performance did not prevent the overall decline in smartphone sales during the opening days. Entry-level devices faced greater pressure because even discounted models were generally more expensive than a year ago. “We had projected a 12% decline in smartphone sales, but based on the first wave of festive sales, we would not be surprised if the decline deepens to around 16%. Platforms have seen strong traffic, but conversions have been weak. Premium smartphones, however, continue to sell well, which could support revenue despite pressure on volumes,” Tarun Pathak, Research Director at Counterpoint Research. Counterpoint also noted that the opening days fell during Pitru Pakha, when some consumers in North India traditionally defer purchases. Navratri began on October 11, after the initial sales period, leaving the full festive effect on offline demand to pay out later. With the online sales campaigns now over, the early figures underline the difficulty retailers faced in converting strong digital engagement into higher-value purchases. Overall, with household budgets under pressure, rising product prices and fewer compelling discounts, shoppers appear to be prioritising essentials and selective purchases over expensive upgrades this festive season. title: [Update] Jio Platforms IPO Subscribed 22.19X On Final Day, QIB Portion Booked 70.55X
content: Update | October 23, 2026, 19:45 IST Reliance Industries’ digital services arm Jio Platforms’ ₹30,213 Cr IPO was subscribed 22.19X on the third and final day of bidding, with investors bidding for 438.26 Cr shares against 19.75 Cr shares on offer, according to BSE data. Qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) led demand, subscribing their allotted portion 70.55X, with bids for 345.76 Cr shares against 4.90 Cr shares reserved for the category. The non-institutional investor (NII) portion was subscribed 14X, receiving bids for 51.04 Cr shares against 3.64 Cr shares on offer. Within the NII category, the portion for bids exceeding ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 15.89X, while the segment for bids above ₹2 Lakh and up to ₹10 Lakh was booked 10.22X. The retail investor portion was subscribed 2.72X, with bids for 23.12 Cr shares against 8.50 Cr shares on offer. The employee and shareholder portions were subscribed 2.93X and 7.60X, respectively. Original | October 23, 2026, 12:14 IST Reliance Industries’ digital services arm Jio Platforms’ IPO was subscribed 6.76X as of 11:48 IST on the third and final day of bidding, with institutional investors continuing to drive demand. Investors bid for 133.51 Cr shares against 19.75 Cr shares on offer, according to BSE subscription data. The overall subscription rose from 5.57X at the end of the second day . Qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) subscribed their allotted portion 14.18X, placing bids for 69.49 Cr shares against 4.90 Cr shares reserved for the category. Within the institutional segment, domestic financial institutions, including banks and insurance companies, bid for 34.51 Cr shares, followed by foreign institutional investors at 26.19 Cr shares and mutual funds at 4.36 Cr shares. The non-institutional investors’ (NIIs) portion was subscribed 9.17X, receiving bids for 33.44 Cr shares against an allocation of 3.64 Cr shares. Within this category, the portion for bids exceeding ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 10.50X, while that for bids above ₹2 Lakh and up to ₹10 Lakh was booked 6.52X. Retail investors bid for 16.96 Cr shares against 8.50 Cr shares reserved, translating into 1.99X subscription. Meanwhile, the employee and shareholder portions were subscribed 2.46X and 5.59X, respectively. Inside Jio’s Mega IPO Jio Platforms has set a price band of ₹1,065–₹1,119 per share for the IPO, which opened on October 21 and closes today. At the upper end, the ₹30,213 Cr (about $3.2 Bn) offering surpasses Hyundai Motor India’s ₹27,870 Cr issue to become India’s largest IPO and values Jio Platforms at around ₹10.3 Lakh Cr (about $108 Bn). Ahead of the public issue, Jio Platforms raised ₹8,109.8 Cr from anchor investors by allotting about 7.25 Cr shares at ₹1,119 apiece. Participants included HDFC Mutual Fund, ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund, SBI Mutual Fund, BlackRock, the Government of Singapore, and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority. The IPO comprises a fresh issue of up to 27 Cr equity shares, with no offer-for-sale component. Jio plans to use ₹27,500 Cr to prepay certain borrowings of its telecom subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm (RJIL), with the remaining proceeds earmarked for general corporate purposes. The debt repayment makes the offering partly a balance sheet exercise, while its growth prospects depend on expanding beyond telecom connectivity into broadband, cloud services, enterprise solutions, and AI. RJIL had 533.3 Mn customers as of June 30, 2026, while Jio’s network carried around 60% of India’s wireless data traffic in FY26. Jio Platforms’ operating revenue rose nearly 15% YoY to ₹1.47 Lakh Cr in FY26, while net profit increased 15.1% to ₹30,049 Cr. title: Unicommerce Q2: Profit Rises 11% YoY To ₹6.4 Cr, Revenue Up 15%
content: Ecommerce SaaS company Unicommerce reported a consolidated net profit of ₹6.4 Cr in the September quarter of FY27, up 11% from ₹5.8 Cr in the year-ago quarter. On a sequential basis, net profit increased 37% from ₹4.7 Cr . Operating revenue grew 15% YoY and QoQ to ₹59.1 Cr during the quarter. Including other income of ₹1.6 Cr, total income stood at ₹60.7 Cr, up 16% from ₹52.2 Cr a year earlier. However, total expenses increased 19% YoY to ₹52.8 Cr, outpacing revenue growth. Net profit growth was supported by a decline in tax expense to ₹1.4 Cr from ₹2 Cr in Q2 FY26. This included a deferred tax credit of ₹1.4 Cr, compared with ₹8.5 Lakh a year earlier. Its adjusted EBITDA for the quarter amounted to ₹10 Cr, indicating a 17% adjusted EBITDA margin. The company said that its profitability had been affected by planned investments in product development, talent, sales and marketing. It expects its profitability to increase in H2 FY27 as “incremental investments moderate”. It added 121 enterprise clients including United Colors of Benetton, Macho, Furlenco, and others during the quarter. It also launched Uniware’s second-generation AI product, DNA, enabling customers to automate operational responses and make faster decisions. The company attributed its growth to continued momentum across its Uniware and Shipway businesses. Uniware, its ecommerce order management platform, recorded 14.5% YoY revenue growth, while Shipway grew 15.7%. “Uniware’s growth trajectory continued to improve, supported by new enterprise additions and increasing adoption of newer modules. Shipway crossed the ₹100 crore annualised revenue run rate milestone, supported by independent customer acquisition and growing cross-sell synergies with Uniware. Our international business also continues to expand profitably,” CEO and MD Kapil Makhija said. For context, Unicommerce is owned by Snapdeal. It offers an ecommerce enablement SaaS platform which enables end-to-end management of ecommerce operations for brands, sellers and logistics service provider firms. Notably, Unicommerce and Snapdeal’s parent company AceVector recently debuted on the exchanges as well. It raised ₹420 Cr via its IPO, comprising a fresh issue of shares worth ₹287 Cr and an OFS of up to 4.16 Cr shares, worth ₹133 Cr at the issue price. While the IPO saw 4.93X oversubscription, AceVector’s stock debuted at an 18.5% discount to the issue price and has seen a cold reception since, trending downwards. Shares of Unicommerce ended the day 4.58% lower at ₹76.09 apiece on the BSE. The post Unicommerce Q2: Profit Rises 11% YoY To ₹6.4 Cr, Revenue Up 15% appeared first on Inc42 Media .

title: Zetwerk Makes Its Market Debut; Can Scale Alone Widen Its Thin Margins?
content: Companies change course in good times and bad. For Zetwerk, the key turn came after it raised $150 Mn from D1 Capital Part­ners in August 2021 when Indian startups raised a record $42 Bn in the calendar year. And what began as a platform to connect manufacturers to vendors and suppliers, turned into a full stack manufacturing play on the back of a bevy of acquisitions in 2021 and 2022 . The company, founded in 2018 by Amrit Acharya, Srinath Ramakkrushnan and Vishal Chaudhary, made its stock market debut today (Friday, October 23) with that full-stack promise at the centre of its pitch. No longer is this a marketplace, but a full-fledged platform that manages everything from procurement, supply, manufacturing, specifications and delivery. While the listing itself was not at a massive premium like some other new-age tech stocks, that’s besides the point when looking at the business model and the sector. The thesis around manufacturing remains strong for years to come as companies in key segments such as electric vehicles are looking to bring more of their component sourcing to India including in vital areas like precision machined parts. This was the opportunity that Zetwerk wanted to capture with its shift from marketplace to manufacturing. In FY26, its revenue from operations rose 40.4% YoY to ₹15,913 Cr, from ₹11,331 Cr in the previous fiscal. Yet, its consolidated net loss widened to ₹1,606 Cr from ₹371 Cr in FY25. This loss includes an exceptional charge of ₹836 Cr from continuing operations and a ₹453 Cr impairment related to its discontinued civil infrastructure business. Those are the realities of working in the manufacturing space. Opportunities come and go and companies have to react in terms of pivoting their operations. The impairment itself is not a major number, but what could worry investors is that adjusted EBITDA stood at a mere ₹421 Cr, translating into a margin of just 2.65% against the revenue. Plus, cash flows present another challenge. Zetwerk’s cash outflow from operations widened to ₹682 Cr in FY26 from ₹386 Cr a year earlier, even as its manufacturing order book grew 43.4% to ₹12,370 Cr. A larger order book offers revenue visibility, but fulfilling those orders requires the company to fund procurement, production and logistics, while managing payments to suppliers and collections from customers. Let’s dive deeper into this as this is what investors will look at. The Two Revenue Pillars Zetwerk operates through two main business segments: manufacturing and ecosystem. The latter operates under the Terra91 brand and supplies industrial raw materials such as steel, aluminium, copper, zinc, lead and bitumen. The manufacturing business, which focuses on custom-made industrial products and related projects, is the largest of the two. Together, the two businesses generated ₹15,913 Cr in revenue from continuing operations in FY26, up 40.4% YoY. Manufacturing accounted for ₹9,375 Cr, or 58.9% of revenue, while ecosystem contributed ₹6,539 Cr, or 41.1%. Simply put, the manufacturing business earns revenue by working with third-party manufacturers and Zetwerk’s own facilities to fulfil orders across energy products, precision machined products and capital goods. Its earnings depend on the price charged to customers relative to supplier payments, materials and fulfilment costs. More complex work, such as precision manufacturing requiring tight tolerances, can command a higher take rate than relatively less complex products. Notably, Zetwerk doesn’t disclose these margins and fees as it is likely to depend on the product and client needs, since this is how the industry functions. In an earlier Inc42 interview, cofounder and CEO Acharya said the company does not consider commission when accounting for revenue. He described the model instead as a take rate for services. He said rates vary across product categories depending on the complexity of the work. The manufacturing segment reported a standalone EBITDA of ₹565 Cr in FY26, translating into a margin of 6.03%. The other side is the ecosystem, which has grown considerably since 2022 as we indicated in the beginning. Unlike manufacturing, where Zetwerk coordinates production, the ecosystem segment aggregates demand for industrial raw materials, procures them in bulk and resells them to customers. Its economics are driven by the spread between procurement and selling prices, after accounting for logistics and other fulfillment costs. The segment’s Adjusted EBITDA stood at around ₹81 Cr, giving it a margin of approximately 1.24%. The thin margin means that changes in commodity prices, sourcing costs or delivery expenses can have a significant impact on profitability, which we will see soon. Plus, the margin is considerably thinner than in manufacturing. These segment-level margins offer a view of Zetwerk’s economics, but the company has not disclosed commission rates or order-level profitability. Zetwerk’s revenue from operations includes the sale of products, income from construction and project contracts, sale of services and other operating revenue. Product sales cover manufactured goods, products sourced from third-party suppliers and industrial raw materials sold through the ecosystem business. Construction and project contract income relates to projects involving broader execution responsibilities, while service revenue includes activities such as job work and related services. Here’s the key difference from any other marketplace: Zetwerk acts as the principal in these transactions rather than simply connecting buyers and suppliers for a fee. It takes responsibility for sourcing, quality and delivery, meaning the revenue it reports reflects the value of goods and services sold, while procurement and fulfillment costs are recorded separately. This is precisely the turn that Zetwerk’s 2021 fundraise and subsequent expansion allowed. Zetwerk’s Big Opportunity Having said that, as we mentioned in the beginning, the problem for the company is that it operates with razor thin margins. Even as the adjusted EBITDA margin has improved year-on-year, it’s still not quite robust enough. Fulfilling industrial orders starts with a substantial procurement bill and procurement costs almost always escalate when there is a disparity in the order book. The key thing for Zetwerk will be to double down in one or two categories which will allow it to maximise the arbitrage revenue. Economies of scale will drive arbitrage revenue in the manufacturing business, especially when Zetwerk owns and controls the procurement side of the business. So manufacturing cannot drive profits on its own and Zetwerk will have to flesh out both sides of the business at the same time. Owning procurement removes third-party broker fees, distributor markups, and structural inefficiencies. The company captures the full margin that middle-men usually take. Add to that, sourcing inputs from low-cost regions which allows you to absorb fixed costs of logistics, customs, and compliance. And as the procurement side of the business scales up, Zetwerk will also have leverage for exclusive, long-term low-price contracts. But it’s not a flick of the switch, buying in extreme bulk can exponentially increase warehousing, insurance, and inventory carrying costs. Moreover, commodity price volatility is another factor since companies can get locked in to massive forward contracts even as market price shifts. So any arbitrage advantage gets flipped here. In FY26, the company spent ₹9,880 Cr on purchases of stock-in-trade and another ₹3,964 Cr on materials consumed, making these its two largest expense heads. Together, they accounted for nearly 86% of its total expenses of ₹16,142 Cr. Purchases of stock-in-trade largely represent goods bought from suppliers and resold to customers. This expense head rose 45.3% YoY to ₹9,880 Cr in FY26 from ₹6,800 Cr in the previous fiscal. The cost of materials consumed includes materials used in manufacturing and project contracts — which increased 31% YoY to ₹3,964 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹3,036 Cr. The two expense heads reflect the procurement-heavy nature of Zetwerk’s business, where revenue growth requires the company to source goods, materials and manufacturing capacity to meet customer orders. Why Revenue Growth Is Not Translating Into Cash Zetwerk’s cash flow numbers point to the pressure of achieving the balance between procurement and manufacturing. In FY26, its net cash outflow from operating activities widened to ₹682 Cr from ₹386 Cr in FY25, even as its manufacturing order book grew 43.3% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹12,370 Cr. A growing order book provides visibility into future business, but it does not immediately translate into cash in the bank. Zetwerk still needs to source materials, pay suppliers and coordinate production to fulfil orders, while customer payments may come in only after goods are delivered or project milestones are met. This gap between spending on fulfillment and collecting revenue can tie up cash as the business expands. The company’s procurement-heavy model means it’s particularly important that Zetwerk gets this balance right. As order volumes rise, the company may need to deploy more working capital to support the procurement, manufacturing and fulfillment needs, even if each order itself is profitable. The challenge is therefore not simply to grow revenue or expand the order book, but to wring out inefficiencies in terms of arbitrage price, production bottlenecks and generally save costs through tech and AI. This will help the company mitigate the risks of delayed cash inflows and receivables. In FY26, Zetwerk’s trade receivables increased by ₹336 Cr, while its other financial and current assets rose by ₹715 Cr. Zetwerk’s ability to improve cash conversion will depend on how efficiently it manages inventory, supplier terms, production timelines, fulfillment and customer collections as it scales. Converting the order book pipeline into cash remains a big test of its business model. Which is why Zetwerk is looking to capture more value by taking on design and engineering responsibilities, rather than simply manufacturing products to customer specifications. Its original design manufacturing (ODM) contracts accounted for 13.93% of manufacturing gross merchandise value (GMV) in FY26. Such work can offer better margins because it involves design and co-development, while also making customer relationships harder to replace. Zetwerk is also trying to balance its supplier network with greater control over complex manufacturing. It operated 26 manufacturing facilities across four countries as of June 2026, while continuing to rely on third-party manufacturers for most of its manufacturing business. Products sourced from third-party suppliers accounted for 80.46% of manufacturing segment revenue in FY26, down from 96.51% in FY24. This suggests that Zetwerk is gradually reducing its dependence on external capacity, but has not moved away from the model that helped it scale without investing in every stage of production. But is scale alone enough to improve profitability? And now as a public company, Zetwerk will have to answer this tricky question. title: Netflix Credits Flipkart Bundle, Indian Shows For Record Q3 Subscriber Additions
content: Streaming giant Netflix recorded its highest-ever quarterly paid net subscriber additions in India in the September quarter of 2026, crediting a strong local content slate and its first transaction-based loyalty bundle with Flipkart. Revenue in India grew about 18% YoY on a foreign exchange-neutral basis, which excludes the impact of currency movements, Netflix said in its quarterly shareholder letter. Viewing hours rose 24% YoY, while viewing hours per member increased by a low-to-mid single-digit percentage. Netflix did not disclose the number of paid net additions in India or how many came through the Flipkart partnership. During its Q3 earnings call, co-CEO Greg Peters pointed to India as an example of how locally produced titles were translating into higher engagement, membership growth, and revenue. Local Content Drives Engagement Lock Upp, Netflix’s first daily reality series, recorded more viewing hours in India than any other title on the platform, measured over its first 91 days. The scripted series Musafir Cafe recorded 9 Mn views, while Operation Safed Sagar clocked 11 Mn views. The India performance formed part of broader growth across Asia-Pacific, Latin America, and Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. Peters said local titles in these regions were driving engagement and business growth. He also said Netflix’s subscriber retention remained healthy across regions. Globally and in the US, churn – the rate at which subscribers leave the service – improved YoY in Q3 and was lower than the company had forecast. Globally, Netflix reported revenue of $12.87 Bn in Q3 2026, up 12% YoY. Operating income rose 37% to $4.46 Bn, while its operating margin expanded to 34.6% from 28.2% a year earlier. For 2026, Netflix expects revenue of $51.1 Bn, representing 13% YoY growth. Neumann said membership growth, pricing, and advertising were expected to support strong revenue growth in 2027, although the company had yet to issue formal guidance for the year. Netflix also plans to introduce its advertising-supported subscription tier in 15 additional countries in 2027, with the first launches scheduled for March. title: Y Combinator-Backed Firstwork Nets $15 Mn To Expand Footprint Across US And Europe
content: US-based HR tech startup Firstwork has raised $15 Mn (over ₹142 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by Earlybird Venture Capital, as it looks to expand its AI-led workforce automation platform across the US and Europe. The round also saw participation from Legion VC and Deel Ventures, along with existing investors Gradient and Y Combinator. The latest fundraise takes Firstwork’s total funding to $20 Mn since its launch in 2024. The San Francisco-based startup plans to use the fresh capital to expand its teams across applied AI, AI research, engineering and go-to-market functions. Important to highlight that about 80% of the startup’s workforce operates from Bengaluru. It also plans to deepen its presence in the US and Europe and extend its AI agents to more workforce operations. Founded by ex-Deel executives Vardhan Kapoor and Shubham Choudhary, Firstwork uses AI agents to automate HR operations pertaining to frontline workers. These include document verification, background and right-to-work checks, onboarding, training coordination, compliance management and worker follow-ups. The startup’s platform integrates within existing HR systems, allowing employers to automate workflows without replacing their existing software. According to Firstwork, more than 1.50 Lakh frontline workers start work through its platform every month. It claims that its platform has helped these customers cut the time spent by workers and HR teams on each new hire by up to 90%. Its clientele features the likes of Deel, Job&Talent, Relay, Wonolo and BGSF. AI is seeing a broad band adoption in the human resource function and is rechanging the face of enterprise tech globally. While Firstwork is primarily targeting the global market, the Indian is projected to double in value to $2.3 Bn by 2033 from $1.12 Bn in 2024. Leveraging AI, several Indian startups are building solutions to capture this booming market. For instance, Bengaluru-based Hunar.AI, which raised ₹40 Cr earlier this week, is using conversational AI agents to automate gig-worker hiring, onboarding, training and employee retention. Its clients include Swiggy, Zepto, Croma, Starbucks and Dr Lal PathLabs. Hyderabad-based TurboHire also raised $6 Mn in a Series A round led by IvyCap Ventures in August 2025 to scale its agentic AI-based recruitment platform. Founded in 2019, the startup automates enterprise hiring workflows and claims to have onboarded more than 120 enterprises, including Cipla, Tata Motors, PwC, Lenskart and Britannia. title: [Update] Tonbo Imaging Shares End Debut Session At 62% Premium To IPO Price
content: Update | October 23, 2026, 16:40 IST Defence tech company Tonbo Imaging’s shares closed their debut session at ₹1,133.65 on the BSE, 61.95% above their issue price of ₹700 but 2.44% below their listing price of ₹1,162. On the NSE, the stock closed at ₹1,133.80, a 61.97% premium to its issue price and 2.26% below its listing price of ₹1,160. During the session, shares touched highs of ₹1,209.85 on the BSE and ₹1,211 on the NSE, representing gains of 72.84% and 73%, respectively, over the issue price. At the BSE closing price, Tonbo Imaging’s market capitalisation stood at ₹6,493.79 Cr ($684.1 Mn). Original | October 23, 2026, 10:00 IST Defence tech company Tonbo Imaging made a strong stock market debut, listing at ₹1,162 on the BSE, a 66% premium to its issue price of ₹700 per share. On the NSE, the stock debuted at ₹1,160, translating into a listing gain of 65.71%. The company commanded a market capitalisation of ₹6,656.18 Cr (about $701.3 Mn) on the BSE at its listing price. The debut followed strong investor demand for Tonbo’s ₹852 Cr IPO, which was open for subscription from October 15 to October 19 at a price band of ₹665-₹700 per share. The public issue was subscribed 135.9X , attracting bids for 115.87 Cr shares against the 85.26 Lakh shares on offer. The IPO comprised entirely an offer for sale (OFS) of around 1.22 Cr shares by existing shareholders, with no fresh issue component. Consequently, Tonbo will receive no proceeds from the public offering. Tonbo’s cofounders Arvind Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar, and Cecilia D’Souza collectively pocketed ₹137.2 Cr by selling shares through the IPO , with Lakshmikumar accounting for ₹80.5 Cr of the proceeds. Ahead of the bidding, the company secured ₹255.4 Cr from anchor investors , allotting 36.5 Lakh shares to 43 investors at ₹700 apiece. Participants included SBI Mutual Fund, Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, and WhiteOak Capital. Inside Tonbo’s Defence Business Tonbo was bought out from Sarnoff Corporation in 2012 by promoters and cofounders Arvind Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar, and Cecilia D’Souza. It subsequently pivoted from research and technology development services to designing advanced imaging and sensor systems for military applications. Its portfolio includes thermal imaging systems, weapon sights, fire-control systems, and missile seekers used for surveillance, reconnaissance, and targeting. The startup handles prototype development, system integration, and qualification testing in-house, while outsourcing manufacturing to partners including Kaynes Technology and Avalon Technology. The strong listing comes despite a decline in Tonbo’s FY26 financial performance. Operating revenue fell 22.7% YoY to ₹362.6 Cr from ₹469.1 Cr, while net profit declined about 30% to ₹50.8 Cr from ₹72.8 Cr. In Q1 FY27, the startup reported a net loss of ₹17.7 Cr on operating revenue of ₹36 Cr. Speaking to Inc42, CEO Lakshmikumar attributed the FY26 revenue decline to delays in executing international programmes , which pushed deliveries into FY27. title: The CFO Code: Perfios’ Prashant Mahagaonkar On Balancing Founder Ambition With Financial Discipline
content: Getting an acquisition across the finish line can take months of negotiations, due diligence, paperwork and financial scrutiny. But closing the deal is only half the battle. The real challenge comes when you integrate the business, unlock synergies, and deliver the value that justified the deal in the first place. Much of this heavy lifting falls on CFOs, who are expected to go beyond balancing the books to evaluate acquisition targets, assess financial risks, structure deals and ensure the business derives long-term value from the transaction. This is part of a broader shift in the CFO’s role, from financial oversight to strategic decision-making. Whether determining how to extract value from an acquisition or assessing if an investment in AI will deliver adequate returns, finance leaders are making critical capital-allocation decisions while ensuring the business stays on track to meet its growth ambitions. At Perfios , a B2B SaaS fintech serving more than 1,000 financial institutions across multiple geographies, Group CFO Prashant Mahagaonkar sits at the heart of these decisions. With more than 25 years of experience across traditional finance, multinational companies, M&A and venture-backed businesses, Mahagaonkar’s career has given him a front-row seat to the changing nature of the finance function. For the concluding edition of The CFO Code series, Inc42 caught up with Mahagaonkar to discuss his experiences and learnings from decades of building finance systems, integrating acquisitions and working alongside founders and CEOs. Speaking with Inc42, Mahagaonkar broke down how his role has evolved, what he has learnt from acquisitions, why CFOs need to question technology spending, and what he believes will define the next generation of finance leaders. Walking The Tightrope Between Risk and Reward Mahagaonkar’s career began in 1999 at Tata Motors, but he soon realised traditional audit and compliance work wasn’t where he wanted to build his career. In 2022, Mahagaonkar joined Givaudan India, a Swiss flavour and fragrance major where he got his first real exposure to what a well-built financial system looked like. For Mahagaonkar, the experience became an education in how large organisations build systems and roll them out across markets. Mahagaonkar then shifted to Essilor India, a spectacle lens manufacturing company, where he was exposed to acquisitions and moved from traditional finance to a more M&A- and business-oriented role. He later joined venture-backed Amba Research, where he raised capital, worked with investors across geographies and eventually managed an exit. Moody’s acquired the company. Mahagaonkar moved to CitiusTech, where he became the company’s first CFO and worked closely with the founder-CEO to scale revenue from roughly $60 Mn to $500 Mn. “Working with the founders to scale the team was a great learning experience for me. I realised how different a founder’s mindset is from that of a professional CEO. Their risk-taking appetite is very different, and they bring perspectives that a traditional professional may find difficult to act on,” said Mahagaonkar. As Mahagaonkar puts it, the experience taught him how to keep the company business-friendly while also protecting it financially. According to him, while founders may be willing to offer more flexibility to win a customer, the finance leader’s job is to ensure the company is adequately protected. “But the solution was not always to take the most conservative position. Instead, the finance team had to establish a playbook that clearly defined what it would agree to and where it would draw the line,” said Mahagaonkar. He added that finding “the art of the possible” within an accepted compliance framework is one of the most important skills he has developed over time. Making Acquisitions Work Beyond The Deal Mahagaonkar’s M&A experience proved valuable when he joined Perfios in July 2025. By then, the company had completed three acquisitions, and his mandate was to integrate the acquired businesses into a cohesive organisation. Perfios acquired an eFRM (Enterprise Fraud Risk Management) business, a segment it had not historically operated in. In another acquisition, it added a collections company, adjacent to its existing loan origination, approval, and credit underwriting businesses. Each acquisition required a different integration strategy. Mahagaonkar shared that his task was to determine what should be fully integrated into Perfios, what should retain its independence and how each business could contribute to the broader ecosystem. All this had to be done while ensuring that every entity remained compliant with the applicable regulatory and reporting requirements. Smaller companies often lack the same level of compliance infrastructure as a private equity-backed or larger organisation. “Therefore, the integration process involved bringing acquired businesses up to Perfios’ standards across areas such as information security, contracts, insurance, risk and statutory compliance,” the CFO said. However, amid all the finance and integration of compliance functions, what generally gets understated and undermined is the integration of people and cultures. Mahagaonkar argues that people integration is also a finance responsibility because acquisitions can easily leave redundant roles and overlapping functions in place. “You need to put it together and be part of those discussions to help and make sure that we build that one organisation which is required,” he said. AI Spend Under CFO’s Scanner The expanding role of the CFO is particularly evident in capital allocation, where Mahagaonkar believes AI has fundamentally changed how technology investments are evaluated and prioritised. “Today, product life cycles have shortened so much that companies may have just six months, rather than two years, to get ahead of competitors before they develop similar products,” he said. For the CFO, this means asking harder questions about whether the company is deploying its capital into the right assets and whether its innovation engine is moving quickly enough to match the pace of competitors. But in this chase, increasing AI spend may seem like the obvious choice for almost every problem, and Mahagaonkar believes companies need to look before they leap. “Not every problem needs AI, particularly when a simple automation can do the job,” Mahagaonkar said. At Perfios, the company has built an ROI matrix around its usage that monitors productivity gains, potential changes in hiring requirements and whether a particular use case should use AI at all, instead of automation or machine learning. Becoming The CEO’s Co-Pilot With the changing relationship between finance and technology, Mahagaonkar believes the CFO has moved from being a backroom player to becoming a co-pilot to the CEO or founder. He also mentioned that being a co-pilot to the CEO does not mean becoming the de facto CEO. Mahagaonkar estimates that around 40% of a CFO’s decisions today require forward-looking judgement rather than relying solely on historical financial data. When asked about the skill sets that will matter most for the next generation of CFOs, he said, “We must accept that today’s young people often know more than we do. They have greater access to information, and they can process and apply it much faster. The real test for the next generation of leaders, not just CFOs, will be managing such high-calibre talent, helping them find meaning in their work and creating an environment where they can succeed.” According to Mahagaonkar, finance leaders of the past could succeed by knowing the numbers better than everyone else, but CFOs of the future will have to understand the numbers, the business, the technology and, increasingly, the people behind the decisions. [Edited By Shishir Parasher] The post The CFO Code: Perfios’ Prashant Mahagaonkar On Balancing Founder Ambition With Financial Discipline appeared first on Inc42 Media .

title: Ola Electric Slides Over 7% After Bearish Call From Goldman Sachs
content: Update | October 23, 16:55 IST Shares of Ola Electric ended the day 6.39% lower at ₹29.90 apiece on the BSE today, while its market capitalisation stood at ₹14,946.06 Cr ($1.58 Bn). The company’s shares are now trading 61% below its listing price of ₹76. Original | October 23, 14:31 IST Shares of electric two-wheeler maker Ola Electric crashed as much as 7.6% to hit an intraday low about ₹29 on the BSE today (October 23) after a bearish outlook from Goldman Sachs. A day after the company opened its ₹1,000 Cr rights issue, Goldman Sachs downgraded its outlook on Ola Electric to “Sell”. The brokerage slashed the stock’s price target to ₹23. It foresees a challenging path for Ola Electric to become cash flow positive given the relatively high interest cost and capex needs of the cell and E2W business. It also cut the EV maker’s top line growth projections by up to 10% for the period FY27-29. The bearish momentum comes a day after Ola Electric opened its rights issue for bidding. Within hours of opening the issue, Motilal Oswal and Calliope Capital Advisors applied for a combined 2.39 Cr shares against entitlements transferred by two promoter group entities — ANI Technologies and Indus Trust. Founder and CMD Bhavish Aggarwal pledged a 4.32% stake in the electric two-wheeler maker to fund his participation in the company’s proposed rights issue of up to ₹1,000 Cr. Ola Electric plans to use the proceeds from its ₹1,000 Cr rights issue primarily to reduce debt and fund business expansion as it looks to strengthen its financial position and move towards cash-flow breakeven. Of the total proceeds, ₹350 Cr has been earmarked for the repayment or prepayment of borrowings, including accrued interest and applicable penalties, while ₹400 Cr will be invested in organic growth across its electric mobility and energy storage businesses. Ola Electric is yet to report its second quarter earnings results. As of Q1 FY27, the company trimmed its net loss by 22% to ₹336 Cr from ₹428 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Operating revenue declined 45% to ₹455 Cr from ₹828 Cr in Q1 FY26. As of 13:52 IST, the stock was down 6.57% at ₹29.87 per share on the BSE, while its market capitalisation stood at ₹14,931.06 Cr ($1.57 Bn). If losses hold, this would be the sixth straight session of the stock ending in red. In the past one month, the stock has lost over 20% in value. title: IPO-Bound Garuda Aerospace’s FY26 Profit Jumps 41% To ₹25.9 Cr
content: Chennai-based dronetech startup Garuda Aerospace reported a net profit of ₹25.9 Cr in FY26, growing 41.1% from ₹18.4 Cr from the previous fiscal year. In terms of operational profitability, the drone maker’s EBITA for the fiscal year jumped 31.8% to ₹35.1 Cr in FY26 from ₹26.6 Cr in the FY25. Operating revenue surged 66.8% YoY to ₹206 Cr during the fiscal under review from ₹123.5 Cr in the previous year. Sales of drones and drone parts brought in ₹99.4 Cr to the top line while the remaining ₹106.5 Cr via sale of services. Another ₹15 Lakh was earned from delivery charges. Including other income of ₹26.5 Lakh, total income for the fiscal stood at ₹206.2 Cr. “During the year, we continued to strengthen our manufacturing capabilities, expand our Drone-as-a-Service (DaaS) operations, deepen our investment in indigenous research and development, and build strategic partnerships in India and international markets. We also advanced our capabilities in artificial intelligence, autonomous flight, data analytics, defence systems and specialised mission platforms,” cofounder and whole-time director Agnishwar Jayaprakash noted in a message to shareholders. The improvement in the financial performance comes as Garuda’s proposed public listing plans take shape. The startup took the pre-filing route to confidentially submit its draft IPO papers with the SEBI earlier in April. The IPO was greenlit by the markets regulator in August. While the startup is yet to file its updated DRHP for public access, its board approved plans to raise up to ₹750 Cr via the fresh issue component of the proposed IPO back in March. As per reports, the OFS component could result in investors offloading shares worth as much as ₹250 Cr. In its annual report for FY26, the startup disclosed that its board of directors had approved a private placement of equity shares worth ₹57.2 Cr back in August. Investors who backed the startup were Umasankar Nistala, Rakesh Pillai, Jitendra Rana, Vimaan Innovators LLP and Aditum Management. The proceeds of the issue would fuel business growth, working capital requirements, and be used for loan repayments. The startup claims to have become India’s largest drone maker, having manufactured and sold over 3000 drones. It also claimed to be the first drone company to partner with three defence PSUs. It has raised a total funding of over $37 Mn to date from investors like Venture Catalysts, We Founder Circle, cricketer Mahendra Singh Dhoni, among others. It was last valued at $250 Mn after raising a $11 Mn Series B funding round led by Venture Catalysts. Where Did Garuda Aerospace Spend In FY26? Garuda Aerospace’s total expenses in FY26 rose 73.2% YoY to ₹172.2 Cr from ₹99.4 Cr in FY25. It reported no exceptional items during the fiscal but bore ₹8.2 Cr tax expenses. Here are the main operational expenses of the startup: Cost of Materials Consumed: Representing the largest operational expense, raw material costs surged 61.5% YoY to ₹116.8 Cr from ₹72.3 Cr in FY25. Impairment Losses on Financial Assets : Impairment losses amounted to ₹11.1 Cr in FY26, compared to ₹6.5 Lakh in the year-ago period. Employee Benefit Expenses: Garuda Aerospace’s personnel-related costs decreased 16.7% YoY to ₹8 Cr in FY26 from ₹9.6 Cr in the previous year. Depreciation And Amortisation Expenses: The cost recorded under this line item increased 13.3% YoY to ₹4.1 Cr in FY26 from ₹3.6 Cr in FY25. Other Expenses: Spending on items like professional expenses, travel, maintenance, rent, and other corporate overheads stayed nearly flat at ₹29.2 Cr. title: WhatsApp, Telegram SIM-Binding Mandate To Take Effect From January 1: Report
content: Messaging platforms including WhatsApp and Telegram are reportedly set to implement the Department of Telecommunications’ (DoT) SIM-binding mandate from January 1, 2027, requiring their services to remain linked to the active SIM associated with a user’s registered mobile number. According to a Times of India report, platforms must complete implementation by December 31, 2026, ahead of the reported operational start date the following day. The requirement could affect users who access messaging apps on phones without the associated SIM. The mandate stems from directions issued by the DoT in November last year under the Telecom Cyber Security Rules, 2024. The original directions named WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, Snapchat, Arattai, ShareChat, Josh, and JioChat. The department said some app-based communication services continued to function without the SIM associated with the registered mobile number being present in the device. According to the DoT, this allowed fraudsters operating from outside India to misuse Indian mobile numbers. SIM binding requires covered services to remain continuously linked to the associated active SIM, rather than relying solely on verification when an account is first set up. The government said the measure was intended to improve traceability and curb phishing, digital arrest, impersonation, and investment scams. The original directions gave platforms 90 days to implement the measures and 120 days to submit compliance reports. However, the government subsequently specified December 31, 2026, as the compliance deadline for SIM binding. Platforms Prepare For Compliance According to a CNBC report, Apple has updated its iOS software to support the SIM-binding requirements ahead of the implementation deadline. WhatsApp and Arattai have confirmed that they are working to comply with the rules. Telegram is yet to clarify on its compliance status, while Signal has not responded to government notices, CNBC reported. Snapchat has reportedly maintained that the mandate does not apply to its service because it does not use phone numbers to identify users. Questions also remain about how individual platforms will support eSIM users. CNBC reported that WhatsApp and Telegram would require a physical SIM card to function, although the precise requirements for eSIM users have not been clarified. The mandate could affect users who access messaging apps over Wi-Fi on phones without their registered SIM, as well as those who frequently switch SIMs. Its impact on access across multiple devices will depend on individual platforms’ implementation. However, the DoT has clarified that international roaming will not be affected as long as the associated SIM remains in the handset. The implementation push comes amid concerns over cyber fraud in India. According to data sourced from the home ministry, Indians lost ₹22,495 Cr to cyber fraud in 2025 compared with ₹22,845 Cr in 2024. In June, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) said Indians had lost around ₹52,976 Cr to cyber-enabled fraud over the past six years, with nearly 8% of the losses linked to digital arrest scams. Speaking at the India Mobile Congress 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi called on global technology companies, financial institutions, and telecom operators to work together to build a comprehensive framework to tackle cyber fraud and deepfakes. “At a time when telecom and digital technology have become so important, it is equally important to make the security framework associated with it ironclad. It is our priority to secure mobile phones and networks,” Modi said, adding that trust was crucial for people using phones to communicate and make payments. title: Ultraviolette Launches New E-Bike X-47 Venom With A ₹2.65 Lakh Price Tag
content: A month after raising $85 Mn, e-bike maker Ultraviolette has unveiled its new motorcycle, X-47 Venom powered by its new VX-100 100V platform. The motorcycle has been launched at an introductory price of ₹2.65 Lakh, applicable to the first 5,000 customers. Bookings opened on October 22. Deliveries are expected to commence in November 2026, the startup said in a press release. The X-47 Venom is the first motorcycle built on Ultraviolette’s new VX-100 architecture. It combines the platform with its new UV LIGHTFURY electric motor and SRB-11 battery technology. It has peak power of 30 kW (39 bhp) and a 550 Nm of wheel torque. The Ultraviolette X-47 Venom is built to have a top speed of 155 kmph. The motorcycle offers a claimed Indian Driving Cycle (IDC) range of 343 km. It can accelerate from 0 to 100 kmph in 5.9 seconds and has a kerb weight of 180 kg, making it up to 20 kg lighter than the previous-generation platform. Ultraviolette Introduces New VX-100 Platform The VX-100 is a new electrical architecture designed to improve energy efficiency, thermal management and charging speeds across Ultraviolette’s product portfolio. The platform incorporates SRB-11 battery technology, which the startup claims offers up to 20% higher energy density and twice the cooling performance. Its thermal management system is designed to dissipate heat up to 50% faster, while the battery pack features a cast-aluminium housing and IP67 protection against dust and water ingress. The motorcycle also features a new motor control unit that is twice as compact and delivers three times the power density, according to the company. “The X-47 Venom reflects our approach to engineering the entire motorcycle as one integrated system,” Ultraviolette cofounder and CTO Niraj Rajmohan said. He added that the modular architecture would allow the company to extend these technologies across future products as it expands its portfolio and global presence. The bike adds to Ultraviolette’s portfolio of high-end, speed focused EV bikes. Ultraviolette’s flagship electric motorcycle lineup is currently anchored by the Ultraviolette F77 MACH 2 and F77 SuperStreet series. The startup is eyeing entry into the EV scooter segment soon, with production of e-scooter Tesseract as well as e-bike Shockwave expected to commence over the next few months. Recently, the electric two-wheeler startup raised $85 Mn (about ₹813 Cr) in a Series E round co-led by Yali Capital and TDK Ventures, to expand its manufacturing capacity and product portfolio, as well as strengthen its distribution network in India and overseas. The startup is bolstering its manufacturing capabilities and plans to invest more than ₹1,000 Cr over the next five years to expand its manufacturing footprint. Its upcoming BIGGA Factory is set to take its annual production capacity to as much as 2.5 Lakh vehicles in the initial phase. Ultraviolette currently has an installed capacity of around 30,000 vehicles annually at its Bengaluru facility, which is being expanded to 50,000-60,000 units. The plant will continue to serve as a manufacturing, engineering and technology hub after the BIGGA Factory comes online. It is also targeting international markets, with exports expected to account for around 25% of revenue over the next five years. title: CoinDCX Admits Losses From Old Wallet Deposits, Denies Breach Of Active Wallets
content: Crypto exchange CoinDCX has acknowledged operational losses after a process meant to secure deposits sent to old, compromised wallet addresses failed, while denying a breach of its active wallets. In a post on X, the exchange said some users continued depositing crypto into addresses compromised during the July 2025 security incident , despite notifications asking them to use updated addresses available on its app and website. CoinDCX said it regularly “sweeps” deposits sent to these discontinued addresses, moving the funds so they can be accounted for and secured. However, this process failed for a period, with the failure identified on the morning of its update. “This failure led to some operational losses, which were absorbed by CoinDCX,” the exchange said. The company did not disclose the amount lost or how long the process had failed. It said all affected users’ crypto deposits had been credited, including those sent to the discontinued addresses. CoinDCX maintained that customer assets remained in segregated cold wallets and that its current central and user wallet addresses were unaffected. It also said no funds from active wallets had been compromised and that trading continued as usual. Denial Followed By Disclosure The update followed an earlier statement in which CoinDCX described claims circulating on X about certain wallet addresses and transactions as misleading. Among these was a post by blockchain investigator Darcy, who flagged transfers of around $16 Mn worth of cryptocurrency from wallets linked to CoinDCX to another wallet. According to the investigator, the funds were subsequently split across multiple addresses and routed to deposit addresses on exchanges including Binance, OKX, and Gate. CoinDCX has not confirmed whether these amounts correspond to the operational losses it disclosed. In its initial response, the exchange said the flagged addresses had been created in January 2025, compromised during the July 2025 hack, and had not been used by CoinDCX since. Cofounder and CEO Sumit Gupta separately denied a fresh wallet breach, saying hackers appeared to be reusing the compromised addresses. Gupta said the exchange had checked its current central and user wallet addresses and found that none had transferred funds to the old addresses in question. He added that the team was investigating further. The subsequent company update acknowledged that users had continued sending deposits to the discontinued addresses and that its process for securing those deposits had failed. CoinDCX had lost around $44 Mn in a cyberattack in July 2025, when an internal operational account used to provide liquidity on a partner exchange was compromised. At the time, the exchange said the stolen assets belonged to its treasury, customer funds were unaffected, and it would absorb the losses. It subsequently launched a recovery bounty programme to help trace and recover the stolen assets. title: From Three Products To 450 SKUs: How R for Rabbit Built A ₹250 Cr Baby Care Brand Around Parents’ Concerns
content: India’s baby care market is growing, and so is the challenge of finding products parents can genuinely trust. When it comes to baby care, Indian parents often look for the same thing: products that are made well, priced for the value they deliver, and worth bringing home. Ahmedabad-based Kunal and Kinjal Popat found themselves at the centre of this dilemma when they became parents in 2011. The couple began searching for a safer alternative, but that search opened another can of worms: finding a product that was safe, well-designed and priced right. Their hunt for safer alternatives soon hit a snag. While there was no shortage of baby products in the market, very few offered the combination of safety, thoughtful design and transparent pricing the couple was looking for. Instead of compromising, the Popats decided to build what they could not find. Kunal brought over a decade of experience across engineering, marketing and sales, while Kinjal, trained in design, brought a different lens to the problem. Together, they set out to make baby products that put safety first with the right price tag. And that is how R for Rabbit came into being in 2014. The couple started with around ₹40 Lakh of their own savings, designing products in-house and working with established, safety-certified manufacturers. “I used to visit factories before finalising any partnerships to ensure quality control, testing and certification standards remain as we want for the brand,” said Kinjal. Initially, R for Rabbit started with three baby-gear products, led by strollers. From there, the company began expanding its portfolio and distribution. Today, the brand controls more than 450 SKUs across categories such as car seats, baby apparel, personal care, feeding ranges, and ride-on toys. R for Rabbit expanded into kids’ personal care by launching the Biomimic baby skin care range in August this year and entered the baby clothing segment with its apparel range in September. As it continues to grow its product portfolio and distribution, getting products to customers efficiently became an increasingly important part of its growth strategy. The company’s partnership with Shadowfax in 2026 reflects this shift, with last-mile delivery becoming a key consideration as the brand scales across markets. Building A Full-Stack Baby Care Brand At the outset, R for Rabbit relied heavily on word of mouth to build trust. Mothers who discovered the brand began recommending its products through WhatsApp groups and personal networks because of the brand’s focus on quality and international standards of safety. This grassroots buzz helped the duo build early sales without leaning heavily on traditional advertising. Thanks to this organic growth, the brand’s portfolio grew to around 25 products by 2016. “Over time, as our range grew, we put a much clearer framework around how we developed our products. We built everything around four pillars: safety, quality, innovation and customer support. For us, the highest quality and international standards are the floor, rather than the ceiling,” Kunal told Inc42. The founders’ focus was clear: the brand’s products should be designed around everyday realities of Indian parents. Strollers, for instance, were designed to fold with one hand, making them easier to manoeuvre in India’s often cramped lifts and busy urban spaces. Similarly, the founders focused on plug-and-play assemblies for parents to set up products without a complicated installation process. They also designed convertible high chairs that could double up as toddler desks. R for Rabbit also began developing and patenting more of its own products instead of selling products already available in the market. This helped the brand carve out a space between expensive imported brands and cheaper local alternatives. By 2019, R for Rabbit built a base of nearly 1.5 Mn parents. From Growth To A More Complex Fulfilment Model The key change for R for Rabbit came when it moved beyond products that parents bought only occasionally. It entered toys with ‘Orapple Toys’ in 2020 and then launched Feather Diapers in 2022. The expansion into new categories also began to show up in R for Rabbit’s business numbers. The company raised its first institutional round in October 2021, and by FY23, its revenue reached ₹128 Cr. It crossed ₹250 Cr in FY25, helped by a wider product portfolio that grew by more than 100 products during this period. Diapers, in particular, emerged as one of the company’s fastest-growing categories, giving the business a more consistent revenue stream. The 2025-26 phase brought further expansion. In August 2025, R for Rabbit raised $27 Mn in Series B funding, led by Filter Capital and 3one4 Capital. In the following year, the company added BioMimic, a biomimicry-based kids’ personal care range, and launched its first apparel line. In 2026, R for Rabbit’s offline reach crossed 3,000 retail touchpoints, while quick commerce emerged as another important channel. As the company added more products, repeat purchases and customers across more markets, fulfilment became a bigger part of the equation. The challenge was no longer just having the right products, but getting them to customers quickly while keeping delivery costs in check. This also meant rethinking how it stored and moved inventory. R for Rabbit eventually moved from a single warehouse to a regional third-party logistics model, bringing inventory closer to customers across different markets. The company partnered with Shadowfax in 2026 to strengthen its last-mile network and offer same-day and next-day deliveries. The primary aim of the partnership was to improve delivery speed and coverage as the brand continues to grow across categories and markets. “We wanted to build a logistics network that could keep pace with our growth and get products to customers faster. As we expand across categories and markets, being closer to the customer becomes increasingly important. Our partnership with Shadowfax helps us strengthen that last-mile capability and improve both delivery speed and coverage,” says Kunal. Shadowfax’s same-day and next-day delivery capabilities have helped the brand reach more pincodes and improve delivery timelines. According to Kunal, the partnership has brought tangible improvement in its turnaround times and greater operational flexibility. As volumes increase, the company expects better logistics efficiency and wider coverage to help it grow revenue while keeping fulfilment costs and operational inefficiencies under control. Faster delivery and broader coverage could also help reduce delivery-related drop-offs and improve the customer experience. Scaling The Next Mile For R for Rabbit, the next stage of growth will extend beyond its existing footprint. The company is looking to deepen its presence in Tier II, Tier III and other emerging markets while continuing to grow in metros. This expansion will bring more customers, higher order volumes and greater demand for faster deliveries, making fulfilment an increasingly important part of the customer experience. “As we work towards becoming a ₹1,000 Cr business, we know that our ability to serve customers across more locations will be critical. Partnering with Shadowfax lets us hold that promise on delivery too, with faster, more reliable fulfilment as we reach deeper into Tier II and Tier III India,” said Kunal. That makes logistics more than just an operational function. Faster same-day and next-day deliveries can improve the customer experience, while better reverse logistics can make returns and exchanges easier. R for Rabbit maintains an overall NPS of 80+, reflecting the word-of-mouth loyalty that has helped build the brand. As the company expands, maintaining that trust will depend on delivering a consistent experience beyond the product itself. By partnering with Shadowfax, R for Rabbit is strengthening its last-mile capabilities to support faster deliveries and wider coverage as it expands into new markets. At the same time, expanding into new markets means R for Rabbit needs to bring inventory closer to customers without allowing fulfilment costs and operational inefficiencies to rise. From three baby-gear products in 2014 to a portfolio spanning everyday parenting needs, R for Rabbit has come a long way. But as the company enters its next phase, the challenge now is to make sure that its products reach customers quickly, reliably and efficiently. title: Swiggy Shares Plunge 17% To 52-Week Low After Q2, Brokerages Cut Price Targets
content: Update| October 23, 2026, 16:32 IST Shares of Swiggy ended today trading session 16.3% lower at ₹176.70 apiece on the BSE. Its market capitalisation stood at ₹48,774.7 Cr (about $5.1 Bn). Notably, shares of the foodtech major have slipped 54.69% below their IPO price of ₹390. The stock listed on the exchanges in November 2024. Original| October 23, 2026 11:52 IST Foodtech major Swiggy’s shares plunged as much as 17.23% to a 52-week low of ₹174.90 on the BSE today, a day after its Q2 FY27 results showed widening losses at quick commerce arm Instamart. The stock pared some losses to trade at ₹181.50, down 14.10%, at 11:21 IST. Its market capitalisation stood at ₹50,099.69 Cr (about $5.2 Bn) at that time. Several brokerages lowered their price targets following the results, citing higher-than-expected quick commerce losses and concerns over Instamart’s growth and execution. However, most retained their existing ratings. Swiggy’s consolidated net loss narrowed 16% YoY to ₹922 Cr in Q2 FY27 but widened 17% from ₹791 Cr in the preceding quarter. Operating revenue rose 36% YoY to ₹7,571 Cr. Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA loss increased to ₹895 Cr from ₹849 Cr a year earlier and ₹778 Cr in Q1 FY27, offsetting an improvement in food delivery profitability. Brokerages Lower Price Targets Citi retained its ‘Buy’ rating but cut its target price to ₹330. It highlighted 18% YoY growth in food delivery gross order value (GOV), alongside margin improvements of 60 basis points YoY and 30 basis points QoQ. However, Instamart’s net order value (NOV) grew around 13% sequentially, below its estimate of 16%, while losses exceeded expectations. CLSA retained its ‘Outperform’ rating but lowered its target price to ₹262. It said Instamart’s 13.4% sequential NOV growth fell short of expectations, while losses were higher than anticipated. The brokerage flagged a widening gap between Swiggy and Eternal in growth and profitability, adding that Instamart needs to deliver consistent improvements to rebuild investor confidence. Nomura retained its ‘Buy’ rating but cut its target price to ₹300. It expects Swiggy’s food delivery business to generate ₹1,300 Cr to ₹1,900 Cr in EBITDA across FY27 and FY28. However, it said quick commerce execution continued to disappoint. The brokerage values food delivery at 40 times its estimated FY28 EBITDA and assigns no value to quick commerce or Swiggy’s cash balances. Jefferies retained its ‘Buy’ rating but lowered its target price to ₹330. While food delivery revenue and EBITDA met expectations, it said reducing quick commerce losses remains critical. UBS maintained its ‘Buy’ rating and ₹375 target price despite describing the results as weaker than expected. Food delivery performed in line with estimates, but quick commerce losses exceeded expectations. It nevertheless noted early signs of a recovery in growth. HSBC maintained its ‘Hold’ rating but cut its target price to ₹240 from ₹315. It said improvements in Instamart’s operating metrics were insufficient to build confidence in Swiggy’s long-term plans, while flagging food delivery market share losses and intensifying competition. Macquarie maintained its ‘Underperform’ rating with a target price of ₹230, citing negative cash flow and intense competition. It said continued spending on pricing and network expansion, alongside monetisation pressures, could delay profitability. Bank of America retained its ‘Neutral’ rating but cut its target price to ₹245 from ₹275. It noted that Swiggy’s food delivery GOV grew 18% YoY, compared with Zomato’s 21.5%. The brokerage also flagged potential cannibalisation of Swiggy’s main food delivery business by its affordable-meals offering Toing, adding that Blinkit’s performance was increasing pressure on Instamart to demonstrate a path to profitability. Instamart’s Profitability Roadmap Instamart reported operating revenue of ₹1,306 Cr in Q2 FY27, up 33% YoY and 6% QoQ. Its segment loss widened to ₹764 Cr from ₹739 Cr a year earlier and ₹651 Cr in the preceding quarter. Despite the increase in absolute adjusted EBITDA losses, its adjusted EBITDA margin improved marginally to -9.7% of GOV from -9.8% in Q1 FY27. Swiggy said it believes Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA losses peaked in Q2 FY27. It expects double-digit sequential NOV growth in Q3 FY27, alongside an improvement of around 100 basis points in adjusted EBITDA margin. Instamart added 1.3 Mn average monthly transacting users during the quarter, taking the total to 14.8 Mn. Orders rose 29% YoY to 130.3 Mn, while net average order value increased 4% to ₹506. The platform added 69 dark stores, expanding its network to 1,240 stores across 133 cities. Swiggy also plans to begin shifting Instamart to an inventory-led model by mid-Q3 FY27 , with the transition expected to take two to three quarters. Under this model, the business will own the inventory it sells. Swiggy expects the transition to improve Instamart’s contribution margin by around 80 basis points and shorten its working capital cycle by eight to 10 days. Meanwhile, food delivery operating revenue rose 22% YoY to ₹2,338 Cr, while segment profit increased 39% to ₹349 Cr. “Our food delivery business delivered its highest ever profits and margins while we continue to unlock new category growth through Toing, our standalone offering for affordable meals,” Swiggy cofounder, MD and group CEO Sriharsha Majety said. title: eMudhra To Exit Certificate Business As Security Flaw Triggers Distrust
content: Bengaluru-based cybersecurity company eMudhra, which recently found itself at the centre of a security key issue, has announced plans to voluntarily wind down its global secure sockets layer and transport layer security (SSL/TLS) certificate business. In a filing, the company said that the decision followed a security incident in which a researcher discovered that the private keys of eight intermediate certificate authority (CA) certificates were weak enough to be recovered. The discovery prompted browser root programmes, including Google and Mozilla, to distrust eMudhra’s certificates, affecting its global TLS business. eMudhra said it revoked the affected CAs within 14 hours of discovering the incident and disclosed it promptly. It added that no end-entity certificates had been issued by the affected CAs, its infrastructure remained uncompromised and no data was breached. “The impact has been quite severe over the last 24-48 hours. Given the risk to the rest of the business and our obligations as a publicly listed company, the board felt it was prudent to withdraw from this business,” Kaushik Srinivasan, cofounder, told Inc42. The company also cited rising compliance costs, declining returns and limited revenue contribution as the reason behind the move. The segment accounts for around 1% of its global revenue. The company reported revenues of ₹701.6 Cr in FY26. The segment’s future commercial prospects also triggered the closure. With Let’s Encrypt offering free TLS certificates and Cloudflare planning to do the same, Srinivasan said the commercial return from the business looks limited, particularly as browser guidelines move towards 90-day certificates. “The board evaluated the social media reaction, but also took cognisance of the ROI, future potential and competitive landscape,” he said, adding that eMudhra would focus on more complex customer problems in areas such as AI and quantum computing. What Does This Mean For eMudhra’s Customers eMudhra said existing customers would be transitioned to alternative certificate providers free of charge over the next three to four weeks, with the company working with other certificate partners to avoid service disruptions. Srinivasan said the distrust of its G3 ECC root had already affected around 30,000 certificates in the US, which were transitioned to its G1 RSA root. To be sure, G1 and G3 are eMudhra’s root certificate hierarchies: G1 uses RSA cryptography, while G3 uses elliptic curve cryptography (ECC). Google and Mozilla distrusted G3 as a precaution following the security incident, while G1 continues to operate and issue certificates. All certificates in India and various adjoining markets were issued from the G1 root. However, the G3 root distrust impacted an undisclosed US client . “It resulted in around 30,000 certificates in the US market being affected because they were under ECC. We had to transition them to RSA. Following our announcement, we have to transition them to another provider. We are actively working on that,” Srinivasan said. The Incident That Shook The World On October 17, researcher Wayne notified browser root programmes and eMudhra that he had recovered the private keys corresponding to eight intermediate certificate authority (CA) certificates. The keys had been generated with insufficient randomness, making them vulnerable to reconstruction. Such keys could potentially be used to issue fraudulent certificates for websites or software, although eMudhra said none of the eight intermediates had issued end-entity certificates. Six were intended for TLS and two for software signing. Browser root programmes from companies like Mozilla and Google moved to block the affected TLS intermediates. eMudhra, at the time, said the certificates were created on April 30, 2025, and had undergone independent audits, though it did not name the auditors or disclose the audit scope. The company said only one affected intermediate was deployed in production, none had issued end-entity certificates, and all eight had been revoked. The incident prompted a worldwide reaction, casting aspersions on eMudhra’s security controls and the reliability of its certificate issuance processes. Security experts were also unsatisfied with eMudhra’s clarification on the matter. Responding to this, Srinivasan said that it was a script error and a human oversight problem; no hardware problem was found. “We will share the facts in due course, and this will also be verified through independent research. It was a one-off, a bad day. That’s exactly what happened.” Notably, the flaw went undetected for around 18 months, spanning two independent audit cycles. Srinivasan said eMudhra will now appoint an auditor to prepare the final report on the incident, which would take 2-3 weeks. Further, the company would strengthen internal accountability, maker-checker controls and independent reviews for critical processes such as key generation. The company is also exploring AI-based checks to detect weaknesses and flag potential errors.
