title: Tonbo Imaging IPO Gets A Strong Start, But Does Growth Justify Its Valuation?
content: From the Iran war to rising geopolitical tensions across the globe, conflicts are driving demand for advanced defence technologies, from thermal imaging and missile guidance to systems that can counter drone swarms. Against this backdrop, Tonbo Imaging’s ₹852.18 Cr IPO offers investors a chance to bet on India’s growing defence tech sector. Bengaluru-based defence tech company’s IPO remained in strong demand on the second day of bidding, garnering 6.29x subscription by 1:30 PM on October 16, according to BSE data, while its grey market premium (GMP) surged to as high as 71%. The Bengaluru-based company has fixed its price band at ₹665-700 per share, valuing it at around ₹4,010 Cr at the upper end. The IPO closes on October 19. The offer-for-sale-only issue comprises 1.22 Cr equity shares by existing shareholders. Investors can bid for a minimum of 21 shares, translating into an investment of ₹14,700 at the upper end of the price band. The company is expected to list on the BSE and NSE on October 23. Founded in 2003, Tonbo enters the market with a specialised portfolio of imaging and sensing systems used by defence forces and security agencies. Its products range from thermal imaging systems and weapon sights to missile seekers and high-power microwave systems designed to counter drone swarms. It claims to have deployed more than 28,000 systems across 24 countries, building a presence in both domestic and international defence markets. However, its recent financial performance has been unimpressive. Revenue from operations fell 22.7% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹362.65 Cr in FY26, while net profit declined around 30% to ₹50.88 Cr. The company also reported a net loss of ₹17.74 Cr in Q1 FY27. CEO Arvind Kondangi Lakshmikumar attributes the FY26 decline to delays in executing international programmes rather than a fundamental change in the business. He argued that defence technology companies need to be assessed over longer periods, given the nature of procurement and delivery cycles. So, can Tonbo turn its tech advantage and order pipeline into sustained growth, while meeting the expectations built into its IPO valuation? But first… A Sneak Peek Into Tonbo’s Tech Tonbo designs and develops electro-optical and infrared (EO/IR) systems, embedded electronics and imaging technologies. Its products help users detect, observe, identify and track objects in difficult visibility conditions. The portfolio spans thermal imaging cores, handheld thermal binoculars, weapon sights, targeting systems, fire-control systems, missile seekers and missile-guidance systems. Tonbo’s technology focuses on reducing the size, weight and power consumption of thermal imaging systems, potentially allowing them to be deployed across a wider range of military applications. “Thermal imaging has been around for 30-40 years. But it has always been heavy, expensive and consumed a lot of power, which limited the applications in which it could be used. What we have been able to do is build components that allow us to reduce the size, weight and power usage of thermal imagers,” Lakshmikumar said. This, he added, creates opportunities to deploy the technology across smaller weapons, helmets and other military equipment. The CEO also sees considerable headroom in India’s thermal sights market as the armed forces expand their procurement of such systems. “India has around 30,000 thermal sights, of which Tonbo has supplied approximately 20,000,” Lakshmikumar said. The company’s RHP, citing a Frost & Sullivan report commissioned by Tonbo, estimates that it accounted for 51% of thermal imaging units supplied to the Indian government between April 2024 and March 2026. Beyond thermal imaging, Lakshmikumar identified missile seekers and high-power microwave technology as two other potential growth drivers. Tonbo is working on a missile seeker programme with Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL). According to the CEO, India has a significant requirement for missiles and Tonbo is the sole-source supplier to BDL for an uncooled missile seeker. The third area is high-power microwave technology designed to counter drone swarms. Lakshmikumar said Tonbo is among a small number of companies globally with the capability to take down drone swarms at ranges exceeding three kilometres. He cited early customer interest, including a letter of intent from Europe and requirements from the Indian Navy, while indicating that deliveries from these opportunities are expected only in FY29-FY30. These programmes offer Tonbo multiple potential avenues for growth, but they are at different stages of development and procurement. Their contribution to revenue will depend on how quickly customer interest translates into firm orders and deliveries. Tonbo’s business model also distinguishes it from a conventional defence manufacturer. The company retains control over product design, engineering and intellectual property while outsourcing large-scale manufacturing to external vendors. According to its red herring prospectus (RHP), it works with manufacturing partners including Kaynes and Avalon. Its international footprint provides another avenue for growth. The company serves customers across more than 24 countries, with deployments spanning markets such as Armenia, Morocco, the UAE, Australia, Europe, the US and Israel. Lakshmikumar said Tonbo approaches international markets with two objectives: using deployments in developed markets to demonstrate technological performance, and entering emerging markets to establish that its products can be scaled at appropriate price points. “We sell to customers such as the Mossad and the US Navy SEALs to show that the products can be technically superior,” he said. Revenue Slows But Recovery On The Cards Tonbo’s financial performance presents an important consideration for investors. Revenue from operations rose from ₹428.19 Cr in FY24 to ₹469.08 Cr in FY25, before falling to ₹362.65 Cr in FY26. PAT rose from ₹68.54 Cr in FY24 to ₹72.76 Cr in FY25 and then declined to ₹50.88 Cr in FY26. The company’s EBITDA fell to ₹104.62 Cr in FY26 from ₹139.06 Cr in FY25. However, its EBITDA margin remained relatively resilient at around 28.9%, compared with 29.6% in FY25. The fall in earnings was therefore accompanied by a much smaller contraction in EBITDA margin, suggesting that the decline in revenue was a key factor behind the lower absolute profit. Lakshmikumar said the revenue decline was primarily caused by international programmes that could not be completed within FY26 and have consequently moved into FY27. “Defence businesses need to be looked at over a three-to-five-year window, and even more so for a defence technology products business,” he said. The CEO cited a programme in Morocco that was expected to be delivered in March but was delayed because equipment required for the contract could not be shipped from the UAE amid the West Asia crisis. Lakshmikumar also pointed to an ongoing programme in Armenia, where Tonbo has delivered systems worth $55 Mn over the past three years. He said the next phase had been delayed because guns supplied by an Indian public sector company were held up, with the shipment route affected by the regional situation. Despite the lower export contribution in FY26, Tonbo delivered gross margins above 51%, compared with the roughly 40% gross margin it typically forecasts for its domestic business. The CEO attributed this to the delivery of a different mix of higher-margin platform systems during the year. The company’s order book provides some visibility into future business. Tonbo had an order book of ₹314.24 Cr as of June 30, 2026, comprising ₹231.87 Cr in domestic orders and ₹82.37 Cr in overseas orders. It also received new orders worth ₹118.15 Cr between July and September, according to the RHP. The June-end order book was equivalent to around 87% of FY26 revenue. While this does not guarantee near-term revenue, it gives investors a base against which to track execution in the coming quarters. Cash generation and working capital are other moving parts of the financial picture. Tonbo reported negative operating cash flow of approximately ₹136 Cr in FY25 and ₹63 Cr in FY26, despite remaining profitable at the PAT level. Inventory rose from ₹219.49 Cr at the end of March 2026 to ₹319.63 Cr at the end of June 2026, while short-term borrowings increased from ₹116.06 Cr to ₹129.72 Cr over the same period. These figures warrant attention, particularly as the company prepares to execute delayed and new programmes. Lakshmikumar, however, argues that the reported working-capital days do not fully reflect the company’s underlying operating cycle because revenue is heavily concentrated in the second half of the financial year. Tonbo’s Valuation Test Tonbo’s IPO offers investors exposure to a specialised defence technology business with proprietary products, international deployments and potential growth opportunities across thermal imaging, missile seekers and counter-drone systems. The company’s position in select thermal imaging categories, along with its existing relationships with domestic and international customers, gives it a platform from which to pursue further programmes. The broader opportunity lies in the growing importance of indigenous defence technology and advanced sensing systems. Lakshmikumar said investors should assess the company based on its proven technology and its ability to sell to demanding international customers. Meanwhile, the company’s high valuation means investors expect it to keep growing quickly. At the upper end of the price band, Tonbo is valued at around ₹4,010 Cr, or nearly 79X of the FY26 PAT. The ~71% grey market premium points to strong investor enthusiasm, with the market willing to look beyond the recent earnings decline and bet on the company’s longer-term opportunity. For investors, the key indicators to watch will be the execution of delayed international programmes, the conversion of new orders into revenue, the contribution of higher-value products and the improvement in cash generation. For now, Tonbo’s proposition combines a specialised technology base with a potentially expanding market. Its ability to turn that promise into consistent financial performance will determine whether the IPO marks the beginning of a new phase of growth. title: ‘Have Never Feared Competition’: Reliance Responds To Elon Musk’s Starlink Allegations
content: Reliance Industries Ltd (RIL) has responded to Elon Musk’s allegations that Indian business interests are blocking Starlink’s entry into the country, saying it has “never feared competition” and that Jio’s satellite services are also awaiting government clearances. The statement follows Musk’s criticism of RIL CMD Mukesh Ambani, whom he accused of protecting his telecom interests and sarcastically described as the “real boss of India”. “At Reliance, we have never feared competition. We see it as the truest test of who serves the customer best,” the conglomerate said. Citing the government’s position that the same approval process applies to domestic and foreign applicants, Reliance said Jio’s own satellite services are awaiting clearances. “We welcome competition in satellite communications, including Starlink. Every player, Jio included, must serve the people of India and abide by the laws and policies of the land,” it added. Reliance also pointed to Jio’s entry into India’s “crowded” telecom market in 2016, saying it has since grown to over 530 Mn customers. It credited Jio with providing affordable data and digital infrastructure, while saying India’s openness to domestic and international investment and innovation rests on the rule of law. Musk initially targeted unnamed Indian business interests, whom he accused of blocking Starlink to maintain their “monopolistic chokehold” on the market. He subsequently singled out Ambani. In another post, the CEO of SpaceX, which owns and operates Starlink, addressed Ambani as “Prime Minister Ambani”. Musk also argued that satellite connectivity could expand internet access in remote areas, where poor connectivity limits educational opportunities and prevents small businesses from reaching global markets. Satcom Operators Await Launch Clearances The Centre has rejected Musk’s allegations of preferential treatment for domestic telecom players, saying India’s satellite communications rules are non-discriminatory. The communications ministry said last week that all three licensed operators — Starlink, Reliance’s Jio Satellite Communications, and Bharti Enterprises-backed Eutelsat OneWeb — were undergoing security assessments and were at broadly the same regulatory stage. The operators hold telecom licences to provide Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite (GMPCS) services using non-geostationary satellite systems. However, they must demonstrate compliance with security conditions before seeking spectrum assignment. A telecom licence alone does not authorise commercial services. In September, it was reported that Eutelsat OneWeb had sought urgent security clearance for its low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellation, having waited more than 18 months since its security compliance demonstration in January 2025. Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi earlier this week, Bharti Enterprises chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal said OneWeb is significantly ahead of Starlink in the approval queue, having applied five years ago. Mittal said its ground network has been ready for three years and its satellites have been orbiting over India for five years. He added that he would be happy if OneWeb received permission even a few days before Starlink. Meanwhile, Starlink has reportedly reapplied to the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) for approval for its second-generation constellation of nearly 30,000 LEO satellites , which is expected to support capabilities such as direct-to-device (D2D) connectivity. Starlink vice president of business operations Lauren Dreyer said earlier this month that the company has established 20 gateway sites in India, comprising hundreds of antennas. title: CERT-In Flags Unauthorised AI Agent Access To Indian Organisations’ Systems
content: India’s cybersecurity watchdog CERT-In has warned that autonomous AI agents deployed for research and evaluation accessed Indian organisations’ live systems without authorisation, reading business records containing personal data and confidential information. In a critical advisory, the agency separately flagged attackers using publicly available agentic AI tools for financially motivated intrusions into Indian entities. The incidents surfaced through AI model providers’ voluntary disclosures, CERT-In’s forensic analysis, and threat hunting. None of the organisations in the voluntarily disclosed cases detected the access themselves. The advisory follows disclosures by OpenAI and Anthropic about agents exceeding their authorised scope during evaluations. CERT-In did not name the providers involved in the Indian incidents. AI Agents Exploit Vulnerabilities At Machine Speed Agents under evaluation accessed information using credentials and connection settings exposed in application configurations, public code repositories, and permissive cloud service roles, exceeding their assigned tasks’ authorisation. Separately, attackers misused AI-native offensive-security frameworks for reconnaissance and financially motivated intrusions. Deployments across infrastructure in multiple countries indicated these tools’ widespread availability. In the financially motivated campaign, agentic tools shortened the time between initial access and an attack’s final impact from days to hours. Multiple agents operated in parallel for hours or days. Organisations that incompletely addressed vulnerabilities faced repeat attacks within days, at greater scale. In the voluntarily disclosed cases, agents rediscovered and reused exposed credentials across separate operations. The weaknesses included exposed credentials; dormant or deprecated internet-accessible APIs; plaintext payment API keys; permissive cloud roles; and exposed administrative interfaces with weak credentials or no multi-factor authentication. CERT-In also flagged unpatched application middleware, saying agents exploited conventional weaknesses faster, more thoroughly, and at greater scale than human attackers. Global Incidents Highlight Containment Risks Earlier this month, the Wikimedia Foundation disclosed activity it believed involved OpenAI agents, including unauthorised wiki edits, unsuccessful exploitation attempts, and millions of automated requests. In July, OpenAI disclosed that models undergoing cybersecurity evaluations bypassed internet restrictions and accessed Hugging Face’s systems. Anthropic has reported similar incidents involving misconfigured evaluation environments. Last week, Anthropic disclosed further unintended actions, including running commands on servers and bypassing controls to access gated data. It said no customer data or internal systems were involved. Against this backdrop, CERT-In has urged developers to isolate evaluations, technically restrict internet access, use synthetic data and credentials, monitor agents live, and automatically stop runs exceeding authorised scope. Developers should block reuse of third-party credentials and promptly notify affected organisations and CERT-In of unauthorised access. Organisations should audit and rotate exposed credentials, remove dormant APIs, enforce least-privilege access and multi-factor authentication, and monitor suspicious API activity. They should retain logs for at least 180 days and treat environments as compromised after credential exposure or confirmed access until forensically cleared. Organisations deploying agents should assign each run a separate, short-lived identity, restrict network access, and maintain tamper-resistant logs. BFSI and fintech entities should also implement CERT-In’s earlier payment and disbursement API security measures. title: Shop Pay’s India Debut, Zetwerk IPO Day 1 & More
content: Shopify’s India Checkout Bet Shopify is preparing to bring Shop Pay to India. Setting up a direct clash with domestic rivals like GoKwik and Razorpay, the Canada-based SaaS giant aims to disrupt the local checkout market on the back of its existing merchant network. Shop Pay’s India Launch: Shopify plans to launch the offering in the country by Q1 2027. The company is in talks with multiple payment orchestration platforms to integrate payment service providers. In India, Shop Pay will likely sit alongside Shopify Checkout as an optional accelerated experience. For context, Shop Pay allows customers to save payment, shipping and contact information, enabling faster purchases across participating stores. The Distribution Edge: What works for Shop Pay in India is Shopify’s existing base of Indian merchants. Since many Indian D2C brands already build their online storefronts on Shopify, the company benefits from deep merchant integration, a ready distribution pipeline and strong global brand equity. This gives Shop Pay a direct route into the checkout layer. Navigating Competition: Shop Pay enters a crowded Indian checkout market populated by established players like GoKwik, Shopflo, Razorpay, Shiprocket and Cashfree Payments. These domestic rivals offer specialised, India-centric capabilities like returns management, shopper engagement and advertising. These may turn out to be a tough nut to crack for Shopify. The Ultimate Test: Shop Pay’s success in India will eventually depend on whether its native integration platform can outperform local checkout rivals on pricing, conversion and localised features. To win, Shopify must prove that Shop Pay can deliver higher net margins and lower overall operational costs than entrenched domestic alternatives. As Shopify gears up to launch Shop Pay in India, can the SaaS giant turn its brand equity and distribution advantage into a meaningful Indian checkout business? Let’s find out… From The Editor’s Desk Zetwerk IPO Day 1 The B2B manufacturing startup’s public issue was subscribed just 23% on the first day of bidding, receiving bids for 4.17 Cr shares against 18.51 Cr shares on offer. The public offer saw the highest interest from QIBs, followed by retail investors and NIIs. Zetwerk’s ₹5,000 Cr IPO comprises a fresh issue of shares worth ₹2,830 Cr and an OFS component of up to 14.45 Cr shares. At the upper end of its ₹143-₹151 IPO price band, the issue values the company at around ₹25,583 Cr. Separately, Tonbo Imaging’s IPO was oversubscribed 4X at the end of the first day, receiving bidding for 3.4 Cr shares against 85.3 Lakh shares on offer. The defence tech startup’s issue consists entirely of an OFS of up to 1.2 Cr shares worth ₹852 Cr. JFS’ Profit Halves In Q2 Jio Financial Services’ consolidated net profit declined 51% YoY to ₹340.4 Cr in Q2 FY27. This came despite operating revenue zooming 73% to ₹1,699.3 Cr in the quarter under review. The company attributed the decline in profits to higher expenditure and the absence of dividend income during the quarter. Total expenses jumped 167% YoY to ₹1,166.1 Cr in the quarter ended September 2026. On the operational front, JFS’ NBFC arm, Jio Credit, had ₹37,320 Cr in AUM at the end of September 2026, while its digital payments vertical clocked a total payment value of ₹14,682 Cr in the quarter. The JioFinance App also reached 3.2 Cr unique users in Q2. Origin Bags $20 Mn The physical AI startup has raised around ₹190 Cr in a strategic round co-led by Accel and Zacua Ventures to build its fleet of robots, support pilots in the US and Europe, and experiment with new use cases. Founded in 2025, Origin is developing modular autonomous robots for the construction sector. Its robots can handle tasks such as drywall finishing, painting, taping, and drilling. The startup plans to deploy 150 bots by 2027-end. Origin operates in the broader Indian deeptech sector, which continues to draw investor attention on the back of regulatory push, subsidies, a thriving talent pool and growing demand. The sector raised $290 Mn in Q3 2026, up 176% YoY. Go Digit’s New Home Canadian investor Fairfax Financial Holdings has proposed transferring its 49% stake in the listed insurtech company to IDBI Bank. The proposed restructuring will make the bank the holding company for the insurance business. This will allow IDBI Bank to distribute insurance products through Digit Insurance. However, the transaction will still require clearance from the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI). The proposals come after the Centre allowed Fairfax Financial to pick up a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank. Under its bid, Fairfax would acquire the controlling stake for approximately ₹52,878 Cr ($5.6 Bn), at ₹81 per share. Udaan’s FY26 Turnaround The B2B ecommerce unicorn managed to narrow its net losses by 19.4% YoY to ₹851.5 Cr in FY26. Udaan attributed the improving bottom line to operating revenue growing nearly 13% YoY to ₹5,134 Cr, tighter execution and EBITDA burn declining about 70%. Despite improving operational metrics, concerns remain over Udaan’s ability to continue as a going concern. At the end of FY26, current liabilities exceeded current assets by ₹1,391 Cr, while total liabilities exceeded total assets by ₹790.9 Cr. Going forward, Udaan said that it is targeting sustained profitability and a public listing, which is targeted for early 2028. To get there, it must sustain revenue growth, keep narrowing losses, complete its debt restructuring and improve cash flows. Inc42 Markets Inc42 Startup Spotlight How Ubiqedge Is Giving Industrial Equipment An AIoT Brain Regulators today expect factories to monitor water extraction, emissions and other metrics in real time. But most of this tracking equipment was never designed to be connected. To solve this, Ubiqedge is building an AIoT layer that automates compliance and operations. A Full-Stack Approach: Founded in 2024, Ubiqedge combines hardware and software to help OEMs and system integrators upgrade conventional equipment. The platform is designed to deliver monitoring and automation without asking factories to replace their existing machinery. The Dual Combo: Its flagship hardware offering, KLEON, connects to industrial equipment, reads sensor data and then transmits it to the cloud. Its SAMASTH software then turns this data into live dashboards, historical records, alerts and compliance reports. For example, KLEON can capture groundwater flow-meter readings, while SAMASTH tracks consumption and can automatically shut off a borewell pump once the extraction limit is reached. The Business Model: Rather than selling directly to factories, Ubiqedge partners with OEMs and system integrators, who bundle the startup’s technology with their equipment. The startup currently serves smart water management, solar monitoring, smart concrete and air-quality use cases. It closed FY26 with a revenue of about ₹7 Cr and cash-positive operations. Growing Steadily: Backed by Piper Serica, the startup claims to have so far served more than 100 direct customers, 8,000+ end users and roughly 30,000 devices deployed through its partner network. The startup now plans to expand into the Middle East. So, can Ubiqedge make industrial AIoT simple enough to move beyond pilots? title: Urban Company Board Clears Plans To Raise Up To ₹2,500 Cr
content: Urban Company’s board today approved a proposal to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr, alongside approving its financial performance for the September quarter. The proposed funding could involve issuance of equity shares, warrants, fully convertible debentures and convertible preference shares. The fundraise will be executed in one or more tranches via preferential allotment, private placement or one or more qualified institutional placements (QIPs), subject to shareholder approval. The final issue pricing and structure is yet to be determined. “The business is materially larger than at listing, growth has stepped up, and we now operate three businesses at scale with proven economics. The proposed raise of up to ₹2,500 Cr is about flexibility: it lets us invest with conviction across each of them, cement leadership in InstaHelp, and pursue inorganic opportunities selectively, without trading off one for another,” Urban Company said in a letter to shareholders. The fundraise proposal comes at a time when Urban Company’s quick home services vertical InstaHelp is facing tough competition from the likes of Snabbit and Pronto, resulting in the prospect of a war for market share fuelled by cash burn . Hefty investments in powering the quick home services vertical is also creating a dent in Urban Company’s bottom line. For the September quarter, Urban Company’s net loss more than tripled YoY to ₹182.5 Cr , while operating revenue jumped 41% YoY to ₹537.29 Cr. Separately, the board also granted in-principle approval to explore residential air conditioners as a new business category under its product brand Native. This would be subject to further evaluations and final board clearances. “This category represents a large market in which the Company already services millions of units annually, providing it with first-hand insights into the existing product gaps and customer needs,” noted UC’s board. Urban Company made its debut on the bourses just around one year ago. Hence, its proposed fundraise puts it among the ranks of several new-age tech companies like Kissht, Swiggy, Ather Energy, and Ola Electric that have sought to return to the public markets for fresh capital soon after their IPOs. On a quarterly basis, its net loss nearly doubled from ₹92.1 Cr. Operating revenue remained nearly flat compared with ₹528.3 Cr in Q1 FY27. The company’s adjusted EBITDA loss for the quarter widened to ₹144 Cr, due to a “deliberate” ₹174 Cr investment in InstaHelp. The company also gave a timeline to improve its bottom line performance in the near future. “We remain on track for Adjusted EBITDA breakeven by Q3 FY28 and Adjusted EBITDA of ₹1,000 Cr by FY31,” it said. title: Ethnic Wear Brand Libas Adds 9 New Stores In Offline Expansion Push
content: Ethnic wear brand Libas is opening nine exclusive brand outlets (EBOs) across five Indian cities during Navratri, expanding its retail footprint during a key festive shopping period. The rollout spans high-street locations and shopping malls in Bengaluru, Jaipur, Kanpur, Noida, and Jabalpur. With these nine new openings, Libas now operates 55+ stores across India. The brand plans to add more than 50 stores in FY27, following 28 openings in FY26 and 10 in FY25. The homegrown brand offers women’s ethnic and fusion wear, including kurtas, suit sets, sarees, lehengas and contemporary Indian outfits. Its portfolio covers both everyday and occasion wear, catering to a range of wardrobes and celebrations. In the women’s ethnic and fusion wear segment, Libas competes with brands such as Biba, Aurelia, W for Woman and Soch. The new outlets are bringing Libas’ collections closer to shoppers, allowing them to explore styles, fabrics and fits in person while extending the brand’s reach beyond its digital sales channel. A Faster Push Into Offline Retail Bengaluru accounts for four of the nine planned outlets at Airport Road, Jayanagar, Commercial Street, and Mantri Mall. In Jaipur, Libas is opening stores at Pacific Mall and Vaishali Nagar. The remaining three outlets are at Z Square Mall in Kanpur, H&S Mall in Noida, and South Avenue Mall in Jabalpur. Sidhant Keshwani, founder and CEO of Libas, said, “As Libas enters its next phase of growth, offline retail will be an important lever in expanding our consumer reach and strengthening our presence across markets. Our focus is on building a retail network that allows us to scale efficiently, respond to local demand and deliver a consistent brand experience.” The company said it crossed an annualised revenue run rate (ARR) of ₹1,000 Cr in March 2026 and is targeting ₹1,000 crore in revenue in FY27. With the nine openings forming part of its broader FY27 rollout, offline retail is set to play a larger role in Libas’ next phase of growth. title: How LeadSquared’s Chandra Sahal Is Turning Finance Into A Real-Time Decision Engine
content: For a long time, the finance function in organisations has been a back-office job — close the books, stay compliant, keep enough cash in the bank to survive the quarter. The job rewarded accuracy over foresight, and a CFO’s standing was measured by how few surprises were brought to the table. The job description no longer holds today, particularly for SaaS businesses, where a small dip in quarterly retention can snowball into a much larger problem. The role has grown to include almost everything under its ambit, from market research to product R&D and even deciding pricing of products or services, once exclusive to the CEO’s role. Simply put: finance leaders are today involved in deciding which market deserves more investment, which product line is worth the losses, and whether a pricing model could open doors to the next big opportunity. In all odds, the CFO today is an organisation’s sounding board. LeadSquared , a SaaS platform focused on sales execution and marketing automation, is also witnessing this shift under the aegis of its CFO, Chandra Sahal, who joined the company in November 2025 after a 12-year stint at Wipro as its head of finance. Prior to joining Wipro, Sahal held key finance positions at Infosys, CRISIL, Vee Healthtek and GOAT Brand Labs. In the 11 months since joining LeadSquared, Sahal has helped the company transition its finance department from a paper pusher (closing books and preparing for audits) to a strategic business partner, where it now has a say in building product roadmaps and driving AI investment decisions. For Inc42’s latest initiative, The CFO Code , we spoke with Sahal about LeadSquared’s finance function, his take on AI, and how finance leaders can become the CEO’s guiding light towards growth and profitability. Assuring Real-Time Visibility Into LeadSquared’s Financial Health Finance teams have long relied on month-end reports to comprehend the financial health of their respective businesses. Sahal has always been obsessed with changing this. At traditional companies, he found it quite difficult to renovate systems that had been embedded for years and brought no benefit. He saw an opportunity at LeadSquared to build systems and processes agile enough to scrutinise the business on the go. For this, he researched and experimented extensively, eventually zeroing in on using SAP, a leading ERP platform, for core financial records, alongside a CRM to track sales and an in-house system to manage the process from order placement to billing and payment. On top of these three layers, he built an internal analytics cum audit system that compiles relevant data to give management a real-time view of what’s happening underneath. “When an invoice is received, it is then looked at by the controller from a revenue recognition perspective and used by the financial team for reporting. All of this happens in real time. We do not wait until month-end to figure out what the revenue is going to look like,” Sahal said. With this, management gets a view into roughly 30% of the month’s revenue in just week 1, 50% by week 2 and 75% by week 3. Therefore, the final week can be spent checking unusual cases and following up with the sales team, instead of trying to scrap the entire month’s numbers, which could be a process prone to errors. Scrapping numbers at the eleventh hour could also jeopardise the finance team’s productivity and create mockery of everyone’s efforts before the CEO. “By month-end, our systems give over 95% visibility into what the final numbers are going to be. This near-real-time reporting assists us in closing books much earlier and getting the management information report (MIS) ready by the eighth of the month,” Sahal said. From Letting AI Do The Grunt Work To Calling The Shots Speaking about how AI has helped Sahal streamline his operations, he shared that everything that is finance at LeadSquared, including reconciliations, identification of journal-entry gaps, variance analysis and budgeting, now has AI behind the wheel. This has helped Sahal do a rolling forecast for the full year by the 10th of every month “So, when I enter a board meeting, I have 80-85% visibility into full year numbers,” he said. So, as someone who keeps an eye on every penny spent in the organisation, how does he analyse the ROI on the company’s AI investments? Sahal has a simple thesis: the return should show up in the team’s productivity. “Faster deployment, faster code checks, quicker product launches and reducing the time spent collecting and reconciling information is where I feel the real ROI lies,” Sahal said. At a time when most organisations think it is a good idea to hire specialised AI talent while bloating token costs, Sahal begs to differ. “The more practical approach here is to train existing employees by investing in their upskilling, be it AI or any other technologies. We, at LeadSquared, have the industry’s best token optimisation practices,” said Sahal. Amid all the AI brouhaha, Sahal does not see AI as a magic bullet but a tool to speed up routine finance work. Tasks that once took days, he said, can now be completed in hours. Similarly, a board presentation that previously took about three days can now be prepared in a few hours. But the bigger shift, according to Sahal, is the unclogged bandwidth his team uses to interpret numbers, challenge assumptions, and focus on decisions that move the needle. Over more than a decade in finance, he has seen several tech cycles emerge and perish. But one thing remains: CFOs need to stay ahead of the tech learning curve. A tech-savvy CFO is a guiding force many organisations lack and don’t even know about. “It is the endeavour of such [tech-savvy] finance leaders that the finance function today has a say at the table,” he said, while illustrating his role as a tech-savvy CFO in the organisation. And ever since the arrival of AI, tracking token usage, the technology stack and utilisation across teams has also become a diligent part of CFOs’ job role, something nobody would have fathomed would be the case a few years ago, according to Sahal. Becoming CEO’s Guiding Force To Defend Margins All said and done, the last 11 months have been anything but a walk in the park for Sahal. He said that when he joined LeadSquared, the company was ailing with challenges that were only patched and never really got solved. Like any other startup, LeadSquared’s focus was centred around growth at all costs. Somewhere along the way, the balance between growth and profitability went for a toss. While such a growth strategy can work for a wide array of startups, the problem is that these fads are hardly sustainable. “Any dollar of new revenue that costs $3 to acquire and churns in a year is not growth. It’s a subscription to losing money,” Sahal said, suggesting the Rule of 40 as a useful gut check for whether a company’s growth rate and profit margin together still make sense. According to the Rule of 40, a company’s combined annual revenue growth rate and profit margin should equal or exceed 40% The second major challenge, he noted, sat outside the company’s control. Sahal shared that LeadSquared was once too exposed to geopolitical unpredictability, which often made its decision-making uncertain while investing in a particular market. “A case in point is our US operations that are averse to rupee volatility. With the INR inching closer to the 100 mark, the onus to defend margins falls on us,” said Sahal. To combat such uncertainties in regional compliance, Sahal has helped LeadSquared partner with vendors that either operate locally in those regions or are based in India with expertise in specific markets. This helps the company cut compliance and other expenses, offsetting INR depreciation in many cases. CFO As A Strategic Business Partner When asked about the mistakes that startups on a hyper-growth path often make, Sahal said that for today’s new-age businesses, an integrated tech stack connecting ERP, CRM, order-to-cash, and an analytics layer is a must. Without an integrated stack connecting the ERP, CRM, order-to-cash, and analytics layers, a new invoice flow could derail projections and create chaos. So, does that mean businesses should build a highly stacked finance function from day one? Sahal argued that early stage startups, with a single product and one geography, have the legroom to operate comfortably on Excel and Tally for a couple of years. “ The trigger for upgrading should be complexity, whether that comes from multiple entities, products or geographies,” he added. Finally, when we asked what the future holds for CFOs, especially in this time and age of AI, Sahal said the role is undergoing a churn and has become too demanding. Finance leaders who can act and play as strategic business partners will define the next phase of finance. The era of just reporting numbers is over, and finance leaders’ new job is to chart the best course for the CEO. title: Urban Company Q2 Loss Widens Over 3X YoY To ₹182.5 Cr, Revenue Up 41%
content: Consumer service brand Urban Company’s net loss has widened 208% YoY to ₹182.5 Cr in the Q2 FY27 from ₹59.3 Cr loss incurred in the previous year quarter. Sequentially, the company’s loss almost doubled from ₹92.1 Cr. The company’s loss widened despite its quarterly operating revenue jumping 41% to ₹537.3 Cr from ₹380 in Q2 FY26. On a quarterly basis, the operating revenue remained largely flat compared with ₹528.3 Cr. Including other income of ₹41.2 Cr, Urban Company recorded a total income of ₹578.5 Cr in the quarter. Its total expenses also increased 61.5% to ₹745.7 Cr in the given period from ₹461.7 Cr in Q2 FY26. The surge in expense was primarily at the behest of increased investment in quick household help vertical, InstaHelp. The company said its adjusted EBITDA loss for the quarter stood at ₹144 Cr, due to a “deliberate” ₹174 Cr investment in InstaHelp. “Adjusted EBITDA was ₹30 Cr, up 213% YoY, and ₹119 Cr over the past three quarters, up 175% YoY,” the company said. The company also incurred a loss of ₹8.1 Cr from a joint venture and incurred a tax expense of ₹7.2 Cr in the quarter. Alongside approving the financial statements, Urban Company’s board also approved a fund raise of ₹2,500 Cr via a preferential allotment or a private placement of equity shares. The rationale behind this fundraise is to strengthen the leadership at InstaHelp, invest across its three major segments, and pursue potential inorganic opportunities, Urban Company said in its Q2 Shareholder’s letter. “We now operate three businesses at scale, with proven economics across India Core, International and Native. We believe each can be significantly larger in the years ahead with adequate investment and high quality execution,” Urban Company added in the Q2 shareholder’s letter. Urban Company’s Three Growth Engines Urban Company is doubling down on three key growth areas: its core home services business, InstaHelp and Native, its in-house consumer appliances brand. InstaHelp, its quick household help vertical, saw fulfilled orders jump 63% QoQ to 6.2 Mn, while net transaction value (NTV) rose 34% to ₹71 Cr. The increase in orders also led to a Operating revenue increased to ₹20.5 Cr from ₹1.4 Cr in the year-ago quarter, but adjusted EBITDA loss of the vertical widened to ₹174 Cr from ₹132 Cr. The company bled ₹279 per order, a 19% improvement from ₹346 loss incurred per order in the previous quarter. Urban Company said it would continue investing in InstaHelp to establish market leadership. The service now accounts for around 45% of new users in micro-markets where it operates alongside the company’s core services. Meanwhile, Urban Company’s India consumer services business, excluding InstaHelp, reported 26.3% YoY growth in NTV to ₹963 Cr and a 28% rise in net revenue to ₹336 Cr. Its international operations in the UAE and Singapore also remained profitable, with NTV rising 66% YoY to ₹267 Cr. Native recorded 35% YoY growth in NTV to ₹132 Cr, while operating revenue rose 40% to ₹105 Cr. Its adjusted EBITDA loss remained at ₹9 Cr, but the loss margin narrowed to 6.8% of NTV from 9% a year ago. The company expects Native’s NTV to grow 50-55% on a combined Q2 and Q3 basis, factoring in the shift in festive demand to Q3. “Growth was healthy but understated by timing: the festive season this year has shifted entirely to Q3, and major ecommerce sale events, which took place in Q2 last fiscal year, have moved to Q3 this fiscal year. It is therefore more meaningful to assess Native across the two quarters together. We expect combined Q2 + Q3 FY27 NTV growth of 50-55% YoY,” the shareholders’ letter said. Urban Company To Foray Into AC Category Besides the financials and the fundraise plans, Urban Company’s board also gave an in-principle approval to a plan to explore residential air conditioners as a new line of business under the Native segment. In its disclosures, the company said that this category represents a large market in which it already services millions of units annually and has accrued first-hand insights into the existing product gaps and customer needs. However, it plans to launch in the category only if it could offer a product that is materially better than existing options. Native’s current priorities remain water purifiers and smart locks, with the company expecting to add at most one new category over time. The company said that it evaluates potential categories based on four factors: the importance of servicing over the product’s lifetime, an unresolved consumer problem that better design can address, a sizeable profit pool with attractive premium margins, and the ability to sell, install and service the product through the Urban Company app using its own service partners. Urban Company said residential ACs fit these criteria. However, Inc42 had learnt about the potential entry into the category earlier in 2025 . As per sources close to the company, its own line of ACs were likely to be launched by early 2026 Shares of Urban Company closed today’s trading session 2.63% higher at ₹158.3 apiece on the BSE. title: FirstCry’s Core Revenue Engine Is Fighting Too Many Battles
content: Sixteen years since FirstCry began its journey, what began as a kidswear marketplace has spawned a massive multi-channel ecommerce and retail empire, and a house of brands that’s grown well beyond kids today. Today, FirstCry is not just a listed kidswear retailer, but also the engine dragging the Globalbees house of brands and a budding education business that will become hard to ignore soon. But how exactly do each of these engines work? Before we dive in, here’s a look at where FirstCry stands after the last quarter, ahead of its Q2 FY27 results. The first quarter (Q1) of FY27 saw its consolidated revenue climb 13.1% year-on-year to ₹2,106.2 Cr, while its overall net losses were slashed by nearly 34%, dropping to ₹44 Cr from ₹66.5 Cr in Q1FY26. According to founder Supam Maheshwari, this milestone marks the company’s strongest baseline revenue expansion over the last five years on a consolidated level. It builds cleanly on the momentum of the previous financial year, where FirstCry closed its books at ₹8,548 Cr in total sales while narrowing its statutory consolidated net loss down to approx ₹204 Cr. However, beneath those headline numbers, take a closer look at the business structure and a different story will unfold. While its top-line revenue signals absolute category dominance, FirstCry’s true bottom line is being heavily squeezed by a highly rigid corporate framework and expensive side-bets. For starters, GlobalBees, FirstCry’s D2C brand aggregation subsidiary, contributed ₹1,894.3 Cr, or roughly 22% of its consolidated operating revenue in FY26 while revenue from international businesses in the UAE and Saudi Arabia grew 10% to ₹947.4 Cr. However, together these two businesses accounted for ₹148.5 Cr in segment losses. Further, in Q1FY27, while India multichannel revenue grew 17.7% and international business rose 12%, GlobalBees remained largely flat. The fastest growth, at 47%, came from the much smaller ‘Others’ segment, primarily comprising the FirstCry Intellitots preschool business. Notably, the segment growing fastest is contributing hardly 1% to the overall consolidated revenue, underscoring the uneven economics behind FirstCry’s expanding revenue base. The Overburdened India Goliath A majority 70% of FirstCry’s consolidated operating revenue comes from its India multi-channel business. In Q1FY27, the segment generated around INR 1456 Cr in revenue, up 17.7% YoY. However, despite operating across 10+ categories for mothers, babies, and kids from conception up to approximately 12 years of age, this revenue channel is continuously losing out on gross margin. In Q1FY27, the gross margin fell to 35.2% from 37.8% in Q1FY26. In other words, FirstCry was selling significantly more but retaining less from every rupee of revenue before accounting for delivery, marketing and other operating expenses. A major pressure point is the diapers business, which although just a 15% contributor to GMV, acts as the primary top-of-funnel customer acquisition gateway. It is a high-volume category hit heavily by quick-commerce and private-label discounting, which temporarily drags down the overall multi-channel gross margins. FirstCry’s parent company, Brainbees Solutions Limited, holds a 76.59% stake in Swara Baby Products Limited, which gives it a promoter status in the company, which is about to go for an ₹1,000 Cr IPO separately. This will allow FirstCry to further vertically integrate its supply chain for the diapers category. To combat the short-term pressures on the diapers segment, Firstcry has been pushing on its private labels particularly Babyhug, Pine Kids, Cute Walk and Babyoye, to gain greater control over product pricing, sourcing and margins. At the same time, FirstCry has been actively pushing efforts around three initiatives. First, it is rapidly deploying internal logistics networks. Its in-house logistics platform RocketBees has scaled rapidly to 72 cities and covers around 50% of total online shipment as of June 2026. In Q1FY27 earnings call, Maheshwari also pointed out a 20% improvement in turnaround time from delivery perspective. The under-3-hour delivery pilot, FC Qwik, is also live across 12 cities completing approximately 1.25 Lakh shipments in June 2026 alone. Founder and MD Maheshwari said, “We had an overall ambition of growing to 10% of our overall shipment onto the FC Qwik platform. Now, we will aim to grow to 20% of our volumes.” He also highlighted that the FC Qwik TAT has been reduced from three to two hours in selected cities and the team is working on further reducing it. As its third pillar, the company continues to be bullish on its physical retail network, which had grown to around 1,190 stores by FY26. Its offline business recorded approximately 15% year-on-year GMV growth in Q1FY27, with management targeting another 90-100 net store additions during FY27. This gives FirstCry an advantage in product discovery and customer reach, particularly beyond large metropolitan markets, but also requires it to manage the costs of an extensive physical network alongside faster online fulfillment. The trade-off is becoming increasingly visible. Despite the 17.7% revenue growth in Q1FY27, the India business’s adjusted EBITDA declined from approximately ₹107 Cr to ₹84 Cr. Its adjusted operating margin consequently contracted from around 8.6% to 5.8%. This suggests that higher sales volumes have yet to compensate for the combined pressure of product margins and operating costs. The company expects some relief as higher raw material and currency-related costs are gradually passed on through product pricing, with a fuller recovery anticipated from Q3FY27, as per management disclosures after Q1. However, competitive pressure in diapering could take longer to ease. In essence, the India multichannel goliath is growing faster, but whether that growth can translate into stronger profits remains the bigger test. The Q2 results will clear up some questions around which direction this key business is headed in. Globalbees’ Drag Effect If the India multi-channel business is FirstCry’s heavy brick-and-mortar anchor, GlobalBees is its high-stakes venture capital pivot. In FY26, Globalbees registered a solid 20% y-o-y growth in overall revenue, however, the momentum doesn’t seem to continue. In Q1FY27, the revenue remained almost flat with marginal reduction, while core categories revenue saw only 2% year on year growth. GlobalBees has been a significant capital allocation bet for FirstCry. Parent Brainbees Solutions earmarked ₹169 Cr from the IPO proceeds for GlobalBees to gain further control of its portfolio under the house of brands model. By March 2026, it had deployed ₹104.81 Cr of this allocation. Separately, in March 2025, Brainbees approved a further infusion of up to ₹146 Cr. Despite this capital backing GlobalBees has not acquired a single new brand since September 2022. During the FY26 earnings call, CEO Anuj Jain acknowledged that the company rationalised its portfolio, cutting off brands struggling with slower growth and persistent losses. Instead, the focus has shifted towards four core categories spanning home improvement, appliances, personal care and lifestyle. Thanks to this, even on flat revenue, the segment delivered a remarkable 308% year-on-year surge in Adjusted EBITDA, jumping from ₹4.1 Cr to ₹16.7 Cr, and operating margins grew from 1% to 3.9%. Jain said the cutbacks are a temporary and planned transition that should be completed in the second quarter and growth should bounce back in the winter months. Globalbees can unlock more growth in these categories, but how profitable will this model remain in the long run? Investors will undoubtedly be looking at the next three quarters keenly. The International & Preschool Hedge The other two parts of FirstCry’s business are part of its vision of targeting customers early and making a global retail giant. The company entered the UAE in 2019 and Saudi Arabia in 2022, betting on far higher spending per child than in India. While average spend per child on its Indian platform is around ₹9,280–₹9,350, the corresponding figures are approximately ₹61,000–₹71,000 in Saudi Arabia and ₹1,60,000–₹1,70,000 in the UAE. But converting that premium opportunity into profits has proved difficult amid aggressive discounting by larger ecommerce rivals. FirstCry has reduced its proposed allocation for the international business after the IPO. The move raises questions about the pace and capital demands of its overseas rollout, even as management maintains that the region remains a long-term opportunity. And to be fair, international revenue growth is in line with the overall topline. International revenue rose 12% year on year to ₹232.1 Cr in Q1FY27, from ₹207.2 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA losses narrowed 22% to ₹16.7 Cr. The adjusted EBITDA loss margin improved from about 10% to 7%. For now, management is prioritising unit economics over a breakneck expansion push and has avoided committing to a break-even quarter. The premium-spending thesis remains attractive, but the international business still has to prove it can turn that opportunity into sustainable profits. Away from the bruising battles of babycare retail and overseas expansion, FirstCry harbors a smaller, highly lucrative engine quietly gathering momentum. Its preschool operations, housed under the ‘Others’ segment, are emerging as an unlikely margin champion in a sprawling consumer empire historically plagued by cash burn. The numbers present a striking contrast. In Q1 FY27, the Intellitots preschool business saw net revenue surge 47% year-on-year to ₹19 Cr, while its adjusted EBITDA improved 65% to hit ₹5 Cr. Operating at a 26% adjusted EBITDA margin, this division outperforms FirstCry’s primary retail segments. With management aiming to scale the network to 1,000 preschools over the next few years, this asset-light education bet offers a clear blueprint for high margin revenue beyond traditional retail operations. But the ₹19 Cr quarterly revenue base is small and the preschool business accounts for less than 1% of FirstCry’s consolidated topline. The profitability offers little immediate relief to the group as a whole. But it could become a bigger lever if and when the core business matures. Is FirstCry Stuck In The Past? When you zoom out, FirstCry’s consolidated revenue model reveals a business in a state of transition, which has not really been solved by its IPO and the funds raised through the listing. It is caught between defensive strategies for margin recovery and an aggressive push for growth. It’s not a crisis by any means but it is a time for the company to reassess its strengths once again and push for growth in that direction. FirstCry is increasingly feeling the weight of over 1,000 physical storefronts, which have saddled the company with fixed, unyielding operational overheads like high commercial rent and retail payroll. The ecommerce moat is also rapidly eroding under a fierce, industry-wide quick commerce frenzy led by Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart and Flipkart Minutes as well as specialised players, which we had reported in detail here . Having gone beyond kidswear and babycare, the harder question in front of FirstCry is whether its disparate pieces can start to show an ecosystem effect to generate enough operating leverage to sustain the business without another major funds infusion, as has been the major trend in the public markets this year for new-age listed companies. title: Now, FSSAI Issues Show-Cause Notices To BigBasket, Flipkart Over Misleading Claims
content: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has issued show-cause notices to quick commerce and ecommerce platforms BigBasket and Flipkart alongside manufacturer Gemini Edibles & Fats India for allegedly promoting misleading claims, “Freedom Cooking Rice Bran Oil”. According to the FSSAI notice, Gemini’s oil was marketed using health-benefit claims, including statements that it “reduces bad cholesterol and maintains/increases good cholesterol” and contains “10,000+ PPM Natural Oryzanol”. Associating edible vegetable oils with heart health is not permitted under the Food Safety and Standards (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018. The regulator claimed that Gemini was selling food products via its proprietary ecommerce website without holding a valid Central Licence covering ecommerce activity. The action follows an examination of promotional material across digital media platforms and ecommerce storefronts. Notably, the FSSAI is mulling the introduction of dedicated regulations for ecommerce and quick commerce platforms as well as cloud kitchens , its CEO recently revealed. The proposed rules would require food listings on ecommerce platforms to display manufacturing and expiry dates and batch numbers online. In this, platforms would be held accountable for misleading claims made by manufacturers. It is also considering mandatory disclosure of cloud kitchen photographs and addresses and stricter checks on dark store storage conditions. This adds to the intensity of the ongoing scrutiny of ecommerce and quick commerce platforms over food safety violations. A few weeks ago, the FSSAI penalised multiple platforms — Amazon, Bigbasket, Flipkart, Swiggy Instamart and Zepto — for allegedly engaging in misbranding, misleading claims, and sale and display of prohibited or poisonous food articles. Earlier in the year, the regulator also issued nine notices to Instamart following consumer complaints over alleged delivery of expired, spoiled, and contaminated food products. Besides, state-level authorities, too, have been cracking down on quick commerce platforms over food safety and hygiene violations at their dark stores. In August, the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) suspended the licences of 14 dark stores after checking 86 such outlets in a state-wide inspection drive. Shortly before that incident, Karnataka food safety officials also sealed a major Zepto warehouse in Bengaluru’s Hoskote over multiple breaches of food safety regulations. title: Cult.fit Gets SEBI Clearance For ₹950 Cr+ IPO
content: Markets regulator SEBI has given its go-ahead to gym chain Cult.fit’s ₹950 Cr IPO about three months after it filed draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) with the regulator. As per SEBI’s latest processing status, the regulator issued its final observation on the offer documents of Cult.fit on October 12. In SEBI parlance, the issuance of final observations signals the regulator’s go-ahead for a company to proceed with its public issue. Cult.fit filed its DRHP in July this year. The company’s IPO will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹950 Cr and an offer for sale of up to 17.86 Cr shares. As per sources, The total IPO size is likely to be around ₹4,000 Cr. Early investors like Temasek Holdings, via MacRitchie Investments, Schroders Capital, German fitness operator LifeFit Group, Accel, Tata Digital and cofounder Mukesh Bansal are among the shareholders who plan to offload shares via the OFS. Cult.fit plans to utilise the funds raised through the fresh issue towards setting up new gym centres, expenditure toward leasing, renting and licensing of existing identified fitness centres, repayment and prepayment of certain borrowings, setting up new exclusive brand outlets, marketing and promotional activities and general corporate purposes. Axis Capital, Goldman Sachs, Jefferies India, JM Financial and Morgan Stanley India are the book running lead managers (BRLMs) to the issue. Founded in 2016, Cult.fit operates a chain of gyms and fitness centres and offers online classes for physical and mental wellbeing. It operated 708 fitness centres across 77 cities in India and had more than ​9.87 Lakh ​paid members as of March 31, 2026. Out of these, 218 centres are owned and operated by the company. The rest are owned or operated by franchises (288 centres) or by independent owners (202 centres). Cult.fit managed to narrow its net loss for the fiscal year FY26 to ₹251.8 Cr from ₹480.8 Cr in FY25. It posted an operating revenue of ₹1,720.6 Cr, up 41.5% from ₹1,215.5 Cr in FY25. The business benefits from a diversified revenue profile, with fitness services contributing roughly 70% of revenues and the fitness products business accounting for the remaining 30%. Cult.fit has raised over $800 Mn to date from investors like Zomato, Accel, Kalaari Capital, Chiratae Ventures, South Park Commons, among others. title: Snabbit Spent ₹16 To Earn Every Rupee In Operating Revenue In FY26
content: Amid intense competition in the quick home services market, Snabbit incurred a net loss of ₹167.8 Cr in the financial year ended March 31, 2026 (FY26) as against a loss of ₹5.7 Cr in FY25. Important to note that FY26 was Snabbit’s first full financial year of operations following its service launch in August 2024. Thus, comparability of the two fiscals is limited. Snabbit posted an operating revenue of ₹12.2 Cr in FY26 compared to ₹26.3 Lakh in FY25. Platform services generated ₹10.8 Cr in revenue, while uniform sales to service professionals contributed the remaining ₹1.4 Cr. The startup recognises platform service revenue net of discounts it bears. Including other income of ₹14.8 Cr, the startup’s total income for the fiscal stood at ₹27 Cr. Interest on bank deposits contributed ₹14.1 Cr, with the remainder largely coming from gains on mutual fund sales. Snabbit held ₹292.2 Cr in cash and bank balances and ₹26.6 Cr in mutual fund investments, totalling ₹318.9 Cr. This balance predates its $56 Mn Series D funding round in April. Founded in 2024 by former Zepto executive Aayush Agarwal, Snabbit connects users with trained domestic help for cleaning, dishwashing, and other household chores, promising arrivals within 10-15 minutes. The April funding round took the startup’s total funding to $112 Mn. It is backed by the likes of Susquehanna Venture Capital, Mirae Asset Venture Investments, Bertelsmann India Investments, Nexus Venture Partners, Lightspeed Ventures, among others. Snabbit currently operates in five cities, including Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Pune and Hyderabad. It intends to expand its operations to 10 cities, with Kolkata and Chennai as priorities. The startup is focusing on penetrating deep into a handful of existing markets , rather than aggressive geographical expansion. Even within cities, it is doubling down on ‘micro-markets’, or certain neighbourhoods where it can ensure quick delivery, rather than the whole city. It was present in 140 micromarkets by May this year, and had onboarded 40,000 professionals on its platforms, with an average order value of ₹169-₹199. Where Did Snabbit Spend In FY26? Snabbit’s total expenses rose to ₹194.8 Cr from ₹6.8 Cr in FY25. Employee Benefit Expenses: These rose to ₹46 Cr from ₹3.3 Cr, including salaries and wages, provident fund contributions, employee stock options, and staff welfare expenses. Expert Service Cost: Its largest expense head stood at ₹63.1 Cr, compared with ₹27 Lakh in FY25. Marketing Expenses: Spending on marketing increased to ₹48.7 Cr from ₹82.1 Lakh in the previous year. Service Fulfillment Expenses: Spending under this head stood at ₹23.8 Cr compared with ₹84.5 Lakh in FY25. Snabbit’s Loss Per Job Falls Below ₹200 In a statement issued today, Snabbit’s CEO Agarwal said the startup closed FY26 with a run rate of 35,000 daily jobs, up 70X from around 500 jobs a day at the beginning of the fiscal year. It acquired nearly 10 Lakh customers and onboarded more than 20,000 service professionals during the year. He attributed the growth to investments in customer acquisition, workforce training, technology, infrastructure and geographical expansion. Agarwal said the startup deliberately invested ahead to scale into the competitive quick home services category. The startup said it closed the fiscal with approximately ₹319 Cr in cash and investments, zero borrowings and a net worth of ₹312.4 Cr. He also argued that its annual financial statements do not fully reflect the underlying economics or maturity of the business. In a separate statement, Snabbit claimed that its losses per job declined from approximately ₹1,500 at the beginning of FY26 to below ₹200 in September 2026, indicating an improvement in unit economics as its operations scaled. Its Q2 FY27 metrics show that the platform completed 64.5 Lakh jobs, up 61% QoQ, and recorded a net transaction value (NTV) of ₹73 Cr, up 34%. House help accounted for 64 Lakh jobs, while more recently launched verticals — home cooking and home salon services — accounted for 50,000 and 10,000 jobs, respectively, in the fiscal. The startup reported an EBITDA loss of ₹145 Cr, equivalent to 199% of NTV. Snabbit also claimed to be the largest high-frequency home services platform by jobs completed and NTV, and the most capital-efficient at the job level. Its strategy centres on building density within fewer cities and micromarkets rather than expanding its geographical footprint aggressively. Competition Heats Up In Quick Home Services Snabbit competes with Pronto and listed home services company Urban Company’s InstaHelp in the instant household assistance market. Pronto closed its $45 Mn Series B round in May at a $200 Mn valuation, adding to the capital flowing into the segment. However, profitability remains a challenge: all three platforms are loss-making due to intense competition, deep discounting, and rising operational costs . Urban Company posted a ₹174 Cr EBITDA loss from InstaHelp in Q2 FY27 , over 4X jump from ₹44 Cr in the same quarter last year. InstaHelp fulfilled 6.2 Mn orders, marking a 63% QoQ increase, while its net transaction value (NTV) rose 34% to ₹71 Cr. However, net order value declined to ₹114 from ₹138 in the previous quarter, which it attributed to competitive intensity and introductory pricing for new users. In the past, Urban Company has claimed that it does not expect InstaHelp to meaningfully contribute to its bottom line over the next 4-5 years. The quick home services segment also faces scrutiny over working conditions. Inc42’s reporting documented workers’ concerns about earnings, strict logged-in hour requirements, and inadequate access to waiting areas and washrooms. title: Rising AI’s Costs Put SaaS Companies Between A Rock And A Hard Place
content: Recently, Zoho cofounder Sridhar Vembu raised concerns over the economics of building software in an AI-driven market. In a post on X, Vembu said server prices have risen 4-5X in a year, while AI usage and token expenditure are pushing up operating costs. Zoho, however, plans to respond by cutting its marketing budget, freezing headcount for 18 months and pausing its usual salary hikes this year. Vembu’s concern is that while AI has made software easier to build, running a software business is getting more expensive. At the same time, AI coding tools and agents are challenging traditional subscription and per-seat pricing models. Another concern, as per Vembu, is that AI-driven productivity gains in software development currently stand at 25% to 50% when measured across the entire product development process. While developers can build prototypes faster, testing, verification and other stages of taking a product to market continue to require human involvement. When AI Costs Start To Bite As AI eats into SaaS revenue, it is also making software more expensive to run. Every AI query requires computing power, adding to operating costs. At the same time, growing demand for AI infrastructure is driving up hardware prices, making it more expensive for companies to run their software. According to ICONIQ’s 2026 data, AI products have an average gross margin of around 52%, compared with the 80% benchmark for traditional SaaS. For established SaaS companies adding AI features, gross margins can fall by 12-17 percentage points, depending on how efficiently they manage AI computing costs. The pressure is also forcing software companies to reconsider how much profitability they are willing to sacrifice to build AI products. On October 15, 2026, SaaS giant Figma’s CFO, Praveer Melwani, said the design software company might not return to its previous gross margins of over 90% as it invests in AI features. Its margins were in the mid-80% range, with the company prioritising long-term growth and competitiveness over an immediate return to earlier profitability levels, according to Reuters . Meanwhile, rather than treating every decline as a problem to be eliminated, some software companies are accepting higher costs, expecting AI features will attract more users, strengthen their products and create future revenue opportunities. Similarly, some are adding more capabilities without proportionately increasing subscription prices. Krish Ramineni, cofounder and CEO of Fireflies, said that the company has not raised its subscription pricing in the five to six years since launching its meeting note-taking product. It is now expanding beyond meeting notes into tasks such as summarising emails, responding to workplace messages and preparing users for meetings, while aiming to include more tools within a single subscription. The Push To Rein In AI Spending The pressure to manage AI expenditure is also showing up in the financial results of Indian companies. Groww, for example, reported a 28% year-on-year increase in total expenses to ₹556 Cr in Q2 FY27, even as revenue from operations grew 47% to ₹1,501 Cr. In its shareholder letter , the company identified inflation in compute costs due to AI adoption as one factor behind higher serving costs. Cofounder and CFO Ishan Bansal said AI-related costs began rising as the company increased its focus on AI, alongside higher compute usage on trading days and a one-off operational expense. Groww expects inflation-driven costs to remain part of its operational baseline going forward. This is prompting companies to re-evaluate their technology investments. Instead of relying entirely on large, general-purpose models, some are fine-tuning smaller models for specific tasks, optimising infrastructure and using more expensive models only when necessary. Perfios, a financial technology company serving banks and other financial institutions, is taking this approach to manage the cost of deploying AI. Sumit Nigam, chief technology officer at Perfios, said the company is fine-tuning smaller language models and optimising model and GPU architecture to make specific workloads cheaper to run. According to him, GPU utilisation costs for some use cases have become significantly lower than the cost of relying on external models such as Google’s Gemini or Anthropic’s Claude. Companies are also looking to improve visibility into how AI expenditure builds up across teams, applications and workflows. On October 12, US-based software company Freshworks signed an agreement to acquire Torii , a software management platform. The deal is intended to extend Freshworks’ Freshservice product into software management and AI spend governance. Torii tracks software applications, licences and AI consumption and attributes spending to the people and teams driving it. The platform is designed to help IT and finance teams understand what is being used, identify cost spikes, set limits and forecast expenditure. Perfios, meanwhile, is combining cost optimisation with closer scrutiny of business returns. Sridhar Narayan, chief business officer at Perfios, said the company tracks profitability at both the product and customer levels. The focus is on optimising costs and directing spending towards areas where it can deliver better business outcomes, rather than cutting expenditure indiscriminately. These approaches point to two parts of AI cost management: making usage visible and controllable, and reducing the cost of delivering each AI-powered task. While AI is making software cheaper to build, the real value lies in data, workflows, integrations and the ability to run business processes reliably at scale. Adapting To A New AI Reality As Indian technology companies head into 2027, they face a two-sided challenge: customers are demanding more productivity from AI, while companies must figure out how to earn sustainable revenues. For IT services firms, this is changing how clients pay for work. A Reuters report found that AI is pushing clients to link payments to productivity gains rather than the hours billed by IT services companies, forcing the industry to rethink its pricing models. For SaaS companies, the challenge is different. As AI makes software easier and cheaper to build, products with limited differentiation risk becoming easier to replace. According to Prashant Singh, the cofounder and COO of LeadSquared, “If AI makes software cheaper to build, then software that was only ever an interface over a database becomes harder to defend. That pressure is real.” But Singh believes the threat is not uniform across the industry. “What is being commoditised is the ability to build an application, not the ability to run a business process reliably at scale,” he said. Proprietary data, integrations and industry-specific workflows will continue to help companies retain their competitive edge. Going into 2027, the challenge for Indian tech companies will be to adapt to AI-driven changes in pricing and customer expectations while protecting their margins.
