title: IPO-Bound Tonbo Imaging Nets ₹255 Cr From Anchor Investors
content: Ahead of the commencement of the bidding for its public issue on October 15, defence tech startup Tonbo Imaging has raised ₹255.4 Cr from anchor investors. According to BSE data , the startup allotted 36.5 Lakh equity shares to 43 anchor investors at ₹700 apiece, the upper band of its IPO price band. Of the total anchor allocation, 21.1 Lakh shares, or 57.7%, were lapped up by 12 domestic mutual funds via a total of 25 schemes. The domestic mutual funds that anchored the round included SBI Infrastructure Fund, Axis Mutual Fund, HDFC Mutual Fund, Kotak Mahindra Services Fund, Mirae Asset, Canara Robeco Mutual Fund, among others. Other investors who participated in the round included Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, WhiteOak Capital, Aranda Investments, Allianz, among others. With this, Tonbo Imaging’s public issue will now go live on October 15 and close on October 19. The defence tech startup’s public issue consists entirely of an offer for sale (OFS) component of up to 1.22 Cr equity shares, with no fresh issue component. It has also set a price band of ₹665-₹700 per equity share for its ₹852 Cr IPO, which values the company at ₹4,009.8 Cr (about $480 Mn) at the upper end of the spectrum. The startup had initially filed its draft IPO papers with SEBI in December last year. It then received SEBI’s approval in July this year. However, the company then re-filed a fresh DRHP in August this year . Founded in 2012 by Arvind Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar and Cecilia D’Souza, Tonbo Imaging designs and develops advanced imaging and sensor systems for surveillance, reconnaissance and other military applications. Its product portfolio includes thermal imaging systems, weapon sights, handheld thermal imaging binoculars, driver-vision systems, targeting equipment, fire-control systems and missile seekers. The startup claims that its expertise lies in blending micro-optics, low-power electronics and digital image processing to produce low-power platforms across visible and infrared spectrums. It counts the likes of NATO, US Navy SEALs, Israeli Defense Forces (IDF), and the defence ministry of Armenia as its customers. At the end of June 2026, the startup claims to have deployed more than 28,000 systems across 24 countries. On the financial front, Tonbo Imaging reported a net loss of ₹17.7 Cr in Q1 FY27 against an operating revenue of ₹36 Cr. For the full fiscal year 2025-26 (FY26), the startup’s revenue from operations declined 22.7% to ₹362.6 Cr from ₹469.1 Cr in FY25. Meanwhile, net profit declined 30% to ₹50.8 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹72.8 Cr in the previous year. title: Scimplify Bags $25 Mn To Scale Its Semiconductor Chemicals Business
content: Speciality chemical manufacturing startup Scimplify has raised $25 Mn (around ₹238 Cr) in a fresh funding round led by Hitachi Ventures, the venture capital arm of Japan’s Hitachi Group. The round also saw participation from existing backers such as Accel, Bertelsmann India Investments, 3one4 Capital and Omnivore. New investors including Teknor Apex, Henkel and an undisclosed Japanese chemical company also joined the round. The startup will use the fresh capital to expand its research, processing and manufacturing capabilities across rare earth and critical metals purification. The funds will also go towards scaling its semiconductor chemicals and battery chemicals businesses. A chunk of the capital will also be used to strengthen SciNode, Scimplify’s agentic AI platform that connects research, process development, control and physical manufacturing. Founded in 2023 by Sachin Santhosh, Salil Srivastava, Dheeraj Dhingra and Hersh Manek, Scimplify is a B2B platform that specialises in end-to-end sourcing and manufacturing of speciality chemicals. It also offers contract research and commercial chemical manufacturing for agro-chemicals, active pharmaceutical ingredients and fragrances. The startup currently operates R&D facilities in Bengaluru and Hyderabad, with its SciNode software platform supporting its manufacturing operations. Its network comprises more than 500 manufacturing partners and thousands of scientists and technical partners. Prior to this, Scimplify had secured $40 Mn in its Series B funding round, co-led by Accel and Bertelsmann Investments, in March last year. “In the 18 months since our initial investment, Scimplify has grown from serving 600+ customers across 16 countries to building a global platform with 1,000+ customers across 40+ countries,” Accel partner Rachit Parekh said. Scimplify’s customers include Henkel, Coromandel, Dr Reddy’s, Coherent, Holcim, BASF, Sanyo, Marubeni, among others. The startup claims to operate across five countries and serves more than 1,000 customers across over 40 countries. Going forward, Scimplify plans to expand its presence in the US, initially focusing on sectors where domestic processing capabilities remain limited. These will include rare earth and critical metals purification and processing as well as high-purity semiconductor and battery chemicals. Scimplify’s latest fundraise comes as India looks to strengthen its position in the global chemicals value chain. Earlier this week, Bengaluru-based speciality chemicals startup NuSynth Technologies raised ₹36.5 Cr in a seed round co-led by Avaana Capital and Shastra VC. Scimplify operates in the broader Indian deeptech sector, which continues to draw investor attention on the back of regulatory push, subsidies, innovative local solutions, a thriving talent pool and growing local demand. Overall, Indian deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 deals in Q3 2026 , a 176% increase from $105 Mn across 29 deals in the year-ago period. The sector outpaced the broader Indian startup ecosystem, where funding grew 5% to $2.2 Bn. title: Zetwerk Raises ₹2,251 Cr From Anchor Investors Ahead Of IPO
content: Manufacturing company Zetwerk has raised ₹2,251.2 Cr from anchor investors ahead of the opening of its initial public offering (IPO) for public subscription on October 15. The company allotted 14.91 Cr equity shares to anchor investors at ₹151 apiece, the upper end of its IPO price band. Domestic mutual funds accounted for around 46% of the anchor book, picking up 6.80 Cr shares through 61 schemes across 22 fund houses. Notably, 40% of the anchor investor portion was reserved for domestic mutual funds, life insurance companies and pension funds. SBI Mutual Fund emerged as the largest among these investors, acquiring 1.02 Cr shares through two schemes. ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund also accounted for around 7% of the anchor allocation. Other participating fund houses included Bajaj Finserv, Abakkus, Baroda BNP Paribas, Motilal Oswal and Edelweiss. Global institutional investors accounted for a significant part of Zetwerk’s anchor book. Capital Group’s Smallcap World Fund Inc received the largest individual allocation, worth ₹288 Cr, accounting for 12.79% of the total anchor portion. Government Pension Fund Global and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority’s Monsoon fund were each allocated shares worth about ₹75 Cr. Meanwhile, Nomura India Investment Mother Fund received an allocation worth ₹50 Cr and ex-HDFC Mutual Fund CIO Prashant Jain’s fund 3P India lapped up shares worth ₹39.9 Cr. Among international investors, the anchor book featured the likes of Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, First State Investments and Societe Generale. Zetwerk’s ₹5,012 Cr IPO will open for public subscription on October 15 and close on October 17. At the upper end of the price band of ₹143-₹151 per share, the offering values the company at a post-issue market capitalisation of around ₹25,583 Cr, or approximately $2.7 Bn. The IPO comprises a fresh issue of ₹2,830 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 14.45 Cr shares, amounting to ₹2,182.3 Cr at the upper end of the price band. The company has increased the fresh issue from ₹2,600 Cr proposed in its updated draft red herring prospectus (UDRHP) . The OFS component has also expanded by 49.2% from approximately 9.7 Cr shares. Zetwerk’s promoters and cofounders, Amrit Pratik Acharya and Srinath Ramakkrushnan, will each sell up to 1.42 Cr shares. Other shareholders offloading their stakes include promoter group entity Creovate Innovation and funds associated with Peak XV Partners, Accel India, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Kae Capital. The company plans to deploy ₹2,160 Cr from the fresh issue towards repaying or prepaying borrowings of Zetwerk and certain subsidiaries. The remaining proceeds will be used for acquisitions and general corporate purposes. On the financial front, Zetwerk’s operating revenue rose to ₹15,739.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹11,331.9 Cr in FY25. However, its consolidated net loss widened to ₹1,606.2 Cr from ₹370.7 Cr in FY25 due to discontinued operations over the past fiscal. The FY26 loss included an exceptional charge of ₹796.4 Cr linked to changes in share conversion ratios and an impairment charge of ₹453 Cr related to its discontinued civil infrastructure business. In Q1 FY27, operating revenue grew 55.4% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹4,117.9 Cr from ₹2,649.4 Cr. Its total net loss narrowed 46.4% to ₹733 Cr from ₹1,368.5 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year. Of the latest quarterly loss, ₹668.9 Cr was attributable to discontinued operations, while continuing operations accounted for ₹64.1 Cr. The year-ago quarter included exceptional charges of ₹803.2 Cr from continuing operations and the ₹453 Cr impairment charge in the discontinued business. title: Jio Platforms Sets Stage For India’s Largest IPO At ₹10.3 Lakh Cr Valuation
content: Telecom giant Jio Platforms has set a price band of ₹1,065-₹1,119 per share for its IPO, which is set to open for public subscription next week. The company is seeking to raise ₹30,213 Cr at the upper end of the price band, overtaking Hyundai Motor’s ₹27,870 Cr IPO in 2024 to become the largest public offering to hit the Indian equities market till date. At the upper end of the IPO, RIL’s telecom arm is seeking a valuation of ₹10.3 Lakh Cr for the IPO. Jio filed its red herring prospectus (RHP) earlier today for its IPO comprising a fresh issue of up to 27 Cr equity shares. Post anchor bidding on October 19 (Monday), the IPO will open for public subscription on October 21 and close on October 23. The telco has reserved ₹500 Cr worth shares for eligible employees, who can avail a discount of ₹54 per share. Additionally, up to ₹2,500 Cr will be reserved for eligible shareholders of RIL. The company intends to utilise ₹27,500 Cr of the fresh capital raised via the IPO for prepayment, in full or in part, of certain outstanding borrowings availed by its material subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm (RJIL). The remaining proceeds, ₹2,713 Cr to be precise, will be allocated for general corporate purposes may fund strategic initiatives, growth opportunities, capital expenditure, working capital, marketing and other business requirements. The issue has no OFS component, meaning existing shareholders will not sell shares through the IPO. RIL currently holds a 66.43% stake in Jio Platforms, while Meta and Google own 9.98% and 7.73%, respectively. title: Infotech Acquires Lightspeed-Backed SaaS Startup Zluri
content: IT advisory firm Infotech has acquired Bengaluru-based SaaS startup Zluri to add the latter’s application discovery, identity governance and administration capabilities to its offerings stack. The terms of the transaction were not disclosed. Following the acquisition, Zluri will operate as a standalone division within Infotech, retaining its product development and core engineering teams in Bengaluru. It will also contribute to Infotech’s newly launched CIO Analytics platform, an API-driven advisory model that combines operational IT data with AI-assisted services and analyst expertise. For Zluri, the acquisition would open a pathway to expand its reach among enterprise customers by tapping into Infotech’s global community of more than 30,000 IT leaders. Founded in 2020 by Ritish Reddy, Chaithanya Yambari and Sethu Meenakshisundaram, Zluri offers businesses a software that helps them track and manage all the digital tools their employees use. These include work apps (Asana, Slack, etc), cloud software as well as AI tools. Its platform also helps companies control who can access what tools, identify unused subscriptions, reduce software costs and protect sensitive company data by removing unnecessary or unauthorised access. Zluri caters to over 250 enterprise clients globally, including Monday.com, Tipalti, Whoop, Catapult Sports, Razorpay, Smartnews, Amagi, Daxko, and Traveloka, and earns over 60% of its total revenue from Europe and North America. It will continue serving existing customers post acquisition. “We started Zluri to give IT and security teams visibility and control over every application and identity in their organisation. Joining Infotech lets us put that data at the heart of how IT leaders make decisions, and we’re excited to build together,” said Zluri’s cofounder and CEO Ritish Reddy. The startup has raised over $32 Mn in funding from marquee backers like Lightspeed, MassMutual Ventures, Endiya Partners, and Kalaari Capital – most recently bagging a $20 Mn Series B fundraise in 2023. Meanwhile, Infotech (erstwhile Info-Tech Research Group) is an Ontario-based IT research and advisory firm that helps organisations improve their tech operations by developing IT strategies with key focus areas like cybersecurity, cloud infrastructure, data and AI. As of now, the firm is seeking to expand beyond its traditional research and advisory business. It claims to have grown by more than 340% over the past seven years and crossed $300 Mn in annual revenue. The deal is in line with an emerging trend of global companies acquiring Indian SaaS startups to expand their capabilities. Most recently, Nasdaq-listed SaaS major Freshworks recently acquired US-based Torii to expand its AI and software spend governance capabilities as well. Besides, software giant Adobe also acquired Peak XV Partners-backed Rilo back in September to build broader marketing workflows for its customers and integrate Rilo’s agentic capabilities into its enterprise suite. title: Jio Platforms IPO To Open For Subscription On October 21
content: Reliance Industries Ltd’s (RIL’s) technology arm Jio Platforms has filed its red herring prospectus (RHP) with SEBI for its IPO which will open for public subscription on October 21 and close on October 23. Anchor bidding for the issue will take place on October 19 (Monday). The company has retained its IPO size as outlined in its draft IPO papers. The IPO will comprise a fresh issue of up to 27 Cr equity shares. As per earlier reports, Jio’s IPO size was expected to be over ₹30,000 Cr. In its RHP, the company outlined that ₹27,500 Cr of the fresh capital raised via the IPO will be uitilised for prepayment, in full or in part, of certain outstanding borrowings availed by its material subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm (RJIL). The repayment will help it reduce RJIL’s net debt and interest costs, improve leverage as well as strengthen its financial position and preserve its ability to invest in strategic priorities such as 5G network expansion, fixed broadband, AI and cloud services, enterprise digital services and international technology partnerships. The proposed prepayment covers three external commercial borrowing (ECB) term loan facilities availed by the company totaling over ₹29,971 Cr. The loans were sanctioned by a consortium of international and Indian lenders including the likes of SBI, Bank of America, First Abu Dhabi Bank, among others and are due for repayment within 2028. The loans were originally raised to fund capital expenditure towards 5G infrastructure deployment and spectrum acquisition. Their scheduled repayment dates fall between March and June 2028. Interest rates on these borrowings range from 1.40% to 5.13% per annum. The remaining proceeds allocated for general corporate purposes may fund strategic initiatives, growth opportunities, capital expenditure, working capital, marketing and other business requirements. The company has outlined the following competitive strengths in the RHP: Technology and innovation: Jio claims proprietary capabilities across network infrastructure, devices, software, operating systems and applications. As of June 30, 2026, it had filed 7,220 patent applications. It also operates an end-to-end indigenous 5G standalone technology stack at a nationwide scale. Scale of digital services: RJIL had 533.3 Mn customers, including 284.9 Mn 5G subscribers, as of June 2026. It had 28.6 Mn JioFiber and JioAirFiber subscribers and held a 61.73% share of net fixed broadband customer additions in the June quarter. Its MyJio app recorded 227.6 Mn average monthly active users during the quarter. Technology-led operations : Jio uses AI-powered network automation, digital twins and its JioBrain platform to optimise network capacity, predict faults and improve service delivery. It said 84% of customer service requests were handled through self-service or AI-assisted workflows in the June quarter. Network infrastructure : The company had access to 3.61 Lakh network towers, over 1 Mn route kilometres of fibre and 26,800.8 MHz of spectrum. Its wireless broadband network covered over 99% of India’s population. The Buzz Around Jio’s IPO The proposed IPO could be among the largest public issues in India. Jio filed its DRHP in June and received an observation letter from SEBI in August . The IPO has also been highly anticipated by investors of RIL. The oil-to-telecom conglomerate said that the IPO will have ₹500 Cr portion reserved for eligible employees and up to ₹2,500 Cr for eligible shareholders of RIL. Earlier, reports said the company has already received more than $20 Bn in bids ahead of the issue, while existing investors, including Meta and Google, are said to be looking to increase their stakes rather than exit. However, the buzz around Jio’s IPO extends to a more fundamental question: can Reliance Industries turn Jio’s telecom dominance into a broader digital technology business that commands a premium valuation? As per Inc42’s analysis in June , Jio’s next phase of growth will depend less on subscriber additions and more on monetisation. With 524.4 Mn subscribers as of March 2026, even a modest increase in average revenue per user (ARPU) could significantly influence earnings. The telecom giant has also displayed robust financial growth ahead of its listing. In the quarter ending June (Q1 FY27), Jio Platforms reported a consolidated net profit of ₹7,764 Cr, up 9.2% from ₹7,110 Cr. Operating revenue rose 11.8% YoY and 2.4% QoQ to ₹39,173 Cr. Meanwhile, gross revenue jumped 12% YoY to ₹45,961 Cr. Beyond telecom, Jio is expanding into AI, cloud computing, data centres, enterprise software, and satellite connectivity. Turning these initiatives into meaningful earnings will be key to establishing itself as a broader digital technology business. title: Google.org Commits $15 Mn To The/Nudge To Expand Credit Access For Indian MSMEs
content: Google’s philanthropic arm Google.org has committed $15 Mn in funding to nonprofit organisation The/Nudge (formerly The/Nudge Institute) to support the growth and digital enablement of Indian MSMEs (micro, small and medium enterprises). The initiative aims to develop scalable AI tools that can help small businesses improve access to formal credit, discover new markets and navigate compliance requirements. Besides, an open call for proposals to identify innovative solutions addressing challenges faced by MSMEs is also on the cards. The initiative also includes a multilingual AI platform to train talent in Tier III and Tier IV towns in job-ready skills and connect them with small businesses. “By partnering with The/Nudge, we are putting open digital tools directly into the hands of small business owners, ensuring that India’s economic backbone is equipped to lead this technology shift,” Preeti Lobana, VP and country manager at Google India, said. The initiative also aims to establish open standards that can help Indian MSMEs become more competitive, creditworthy and visible in global markets. The funding comes amid growing efforts to leverage AI for improving productivity and expanding access to digital services among small businesses. For MSMEs, AI-powered tools could help simplify operational processes, improve access to information and address some of the barriers that limit their ability to scale. India’s MSME sector continues to face structural challenges in accessing formal finance, expanding market reach and navigating compliance requirements. For smaller enterprises, limited access to business information and digital tools can further complicate these processes. A World Economic Forum report published in October 2025 estimated that AI adoption could unlock $490-685 Bn in economic value for India’s MSME sector. Amid this, digital lenders have increased focus on MSMEs, which often have difficulty in raising formal credit despite being the country’s second largest employer. New-age NBFCs like Indifi Capital, Techfino, Lendingkart, FlexiLoans, Aye Finance, among others, are leveraging tech to address this issue and provide credit to MSMEs. Prior to this, Google.org announced a $1 Mn grant to help improve news literacy in India and fight back against misinformation and fake news, in 2020. It has also given a grant of $3 Mn to non-profit organisations in India in 2018, to provide quality education in India through elearning. title: Parallel Loop Raises $6.6 Mn To Integrate AI Into Enterprise Workflows
content: Enterprise AI startup Parallel Loop has raised $6.6 Mn (about ₹63.1 Cr) in a seed funding round led by 3one4 Capital, with participation from Picus Capital, Flourish Ventures, and Economic Development Innovations Singapore. Paytm founder Vijay Shekhar Sharma, CRED founder Kunal Shah, and former Singapore Economic Development Board chairman Philip Yeo also participated in the round, among others. The startup plans to use the capital to strengthen its go-to-market strategy, expand its team, and scale operations, with a focus on Western markets, cofounder Prateek Jogani told Inc42. Founded in June this year by Jogani and Yujun Chean, Parallel Loop helps mid-market and large enterprises integrate AI into their existing technology systems, processes, and workflows. The US-headquartered startup has an entity in Bengaluru, with 85-90% of its workforce based in India, Jogani said. It has a team of 30 across Singapore, Bengaluru, Bangkok, London, and Dubai, and works with more than 12 enterprises globally. Its clients include Licious and Havells in India, and Tokio Marine Safety Insurance in Thailand. Jogani and Chean previously cofounded FairDee, a Thailand-based insurtech startup acquired by Qoala. At Qoala, Jogani served as group chief technology officer, while Chean was group chief operating officer. They helped scale the business across five Southeast Asian markets. Parallel Loop’s Enterprise AI Play Parallel Loop combines its AI platform with engineering teams that work alongside clients to identify use cases, integrate AI into existing systems, and build customised workflows and applications. It describes this combination of software infrastructure and engineering support as an “AI operating partner” model. Its offerings span AI enablement, an AI stack, and a software factory. The AI enablement service helps leadership teams identify use cases and develop adoption roadmaps, while the AI stack connects existing systems and organisational data to power dashboards and automated workflows. The software factory focuses on modernising legacy systems and building new applications. Enterprises can deploy the platform in their own cloud environment or on-premises, retaining control over data access and residency. It supports multiple AI model providers, including open-weight models. Within these deployments, Jogani said the startup focuses on deterministic workflows in which steps follow pre-defined rules, rather than autonomous AI agents that execute tasks independently. It uses AI to develop workflows but codifies most steps, reserving AI-based decisions for tasks requiring classification or judgement. Such tasks account for around 10% of a workflow, he said. At Havells, several hundred employees already use the platform for workflows, automations, and dashboards, according to the startup. Parallel Loop is also working with the electrical equipment maker to improve coordination among sales teams, channel partners, and influencers through AI-powered insights. Parallel Loop’s fundraise comes amid investor interest in startups applying AI to enterprise workflows. Yesterday, Clueso raised $10 Mn in a Series A round led by Dharana Capital to expand its platform for creating and updating business videos using AI agents. The opportunity extends across enterprise functions as businesses move beyond AI pilots to production deployments. According to Google and Inc42’s ’Bharat AI Startups Report 2026’ , India’s enterprise AI market is projected to grow to $71 Bn by 2030. title: How Fix My Curls Built Its Quick Commerce Engine From Scratch
content: For as long as Anshita Mehrotra can remember, conversations at her home were all about cosmetic formulations, ingredients, and consumer behaviour. For Mehrotras, beauty wasn’t just another industry but a family business. Her mother, Shailey Malhotra, had built Fixderma into one of India’s trusted skincare brands, serving millions of consumers. And the obvious path for Anshita was to step into an already successful business. Instead, she chose a road less trodden. After graduating in Canada and returning to India in 2018, Mehrotra began exploring a gap in the beauty market that’s worth tapping into. And it didn’t take long to find one. Like millions of Indians with naturally curly hair, she knew the daily struggle of keeping her textured hair hydrated. The products available in the market largely revolved around oils, which moisturised but often left hair greasy and difficult to manage. There was little available that could hydrate curls, style them, be used daily, and still feel light and smell good. The market was dominated by expensive salon-grade products that were not suitable for daily use. “There was no curl cream or shampoo for hair like mine. The market simply didn’t exist, and there was a huge unmet need staring us in the face, and I knew I could build in that space,” Anshita Mehrotra, founder of Fix My Curls, told Inc42. Having grown up around the beauty industry, she understood the product development process, knew the experts she needed to work with, and had access to manufacturing capabilities. After almost eight months working with hair care specialists, she developed what she says was the category’s first leave-in curl cream and hair gel specifically for the Indian market. The products were free from sulfates, silicones, parabens, mineral oils, and drying alcohols, and promised an everyday styling routine. In 2019, Mehrotra launched Fix My Curls through its own website, followed by an Amazon listing. But just as the business was finding its footing, the pandemic brought the industry, like much of the world, to a standstill. “It was a difficult year for sales. But with everyone spending more time on their phones, I realised that if I couldn’t get the product into their hands, I could at least help them understand why they needed it,” Mehrotra said, sharing that within the first lockdown, her educational content led the brand to gain over 12,000 active followers on Instagram. After 2021, Fix My Curls began operating independently of Fixderma and expanded its presence across beauty-focussed marketplaces such as Nykaa, Vanity Wagon, and Sublime Life. According to Mehrotra, that was when the brand found its first real product-market fit. And the next chapter of growth began with a bet on quick commerce. Fix My Curls first entered quick commerce in the second half of 2023 with a limited rollout across a handful of Blinkit pin codes. We were trying to reach out to a new customer base that ordered more frequently. “We were among the first personal care brands to bet on quick commerce. It was challenging because neither Blinkit nor we had a playbook. We were figuring out purchase orders and operations as we went,” Mehrotra told Inc42. The breakthrough came in January 2024, when Blinkit expanded the brand’s presence nationwide. And by then, Mehrotra’s years of educating consumers online had created a loyal audience that was ready to buy. Today, quick commerce is among the largest contributors to Fix My Curls’ total sales. Marketplaces and quick commerce account for nearly 70% of the brand’s total sales, while its D2C website contributes around 25%. The remaining 5% comes from exports to markets including Nepal, Switzerland, Malaysia and Romania. While Fix My Curls reported revenue of over ₹21.42 Cr in FY25, it is yet to turn profitable. According to Mehrotra, the company expects to achieve EBITDA profitability of 2-5% in FY27. As it works toward that goal, quick commerce is increasingly emerging as a profitable channel, and during our conversation, Mehrotra shared the lessons she learned over the last three years of building in quick commerce that helped the brand crack the channel. Overcoming Q-Comm Challenges According to Mehrotra, the initial few months in 2023 were challenging. The team was trying to identify the right hero product, determine its pricing, and decide which cities to launch in first. Because the category was new to the platform, Blinkit had no historical data to show which products would sell, how often they would need replenishment, or what consumer behaviour to expect. But now that the company is three years into quick-commerce operations, it has a clear list of dos and don’ts. Building For Q-Comm Cart Behaviour Without a proven framework, Fix My Curls leaned back on its most trusted signal: customer data. Fix My Curls used performance metrics from its hero SKUs on Amazon and its website to decide which products to list first on Blinkit. It also ran self-funded Meta campaigns to spread awareness that they were now available on Q-comm, too. “We would make ads just to tell people that our products were available on Blinkit. Nobody asked us to do it. We did it because we knew we needed to increase awareness,” Mehrotra said. But the brand soon realised that the channel was highly price sensitive. Blinkit users weren’t necessarily willing to spend ₹700-₹800 on haircare while ordering groceries. Cart context and purchase intent were fundamentally different. “We realised that if somebody is adding groceries worth ₹1,000 to ₹1,500, our product needs to feel like an easy addition to that cart,” Mehrotra explained. In response, Fix My Curls designed smaller trial and travel packs priced between ₹150 and ₹300, which helped the brand sell quickly and maintain smaller but frequent POs. Catching Replenishment Rhythm For Fix My Curls, Q-comm widened execution challenges that didn’t exist in traditional ecommerce. Mehrotra noted that, unlike ecommerce channels, where inventory cycles are relatively predictable, quick commerce operates on tight replenishment windows of just four to seven days. “The biggest thing we struggled with was that we just weren’t able to fulfil purchase orders fast enough,” Mehrotra said. To deal with this, Mehrotra built a dedicated quick commerce function. One team member was assigned exclusively to the channel and is responsible for tracking SKU-level demand daily and maintaining inventory buffers above projected needs. The brand also began closely monitoring daily run rates and planning inventory 15% to 20% above forecasts. However, according to Mehrotra, inventory planning continues to be tested during new product launches, when demand can far exceed projections. She recalled that the quick commerce version of the Milky Leave-In Serum sold out almost immediately after launch, forcing the company to place “three separate purchase orders in quick succession” to keep up with demand. Mehrotra also shared that getting POs delivered on time to fulfilment centres was another critical factor, as larger logistics partners, she found, were often too stretched across clients to handle Fix My Curls’ tight replenishment cycles. Smaller logistics partners, however, proved more responsive and reliable. “The biggest thing is that you cannot miss your purchase order, and to make sure you don’t, you have to find the right logistics partner,” she added. Building For Q-Comm’s Search Intent Eventually, Mehrotra also realised that quick commerce shoppers were fundamentally different in their shopping habits. Unlike Instagram or a brand website, where consumers often come with a specific intent, quick commerce is driven largely by searching for a specific product. “People were not searching for Fix My Curls. They were searching for products like shampoo, gel or dry shampoo,” she said. To accommodate that insight into the product, Fix My Curls worked with quick commerce partners to shape the final form of their dry shampoo. The data showed that customers on the channel wanted travel-friendly haircare, so the brand launched a version that was compact, competitively priced, and under 100 ml. According to the founder, these minor product changes drastically impacted sales, and the company now works closely with quick commerce platforms while developing new products. Fix My Curls’ experience reflects a wider discovery challenge for haircare brands on quick commerce. Being available on a platform is only the first step. How consistently products remain in stock, where they appear in search results, how much shelf visibility they receive and how their prices compare with competitors can also influence their chances of discovery. Future Growth For Fix My Curls’ Q-Comm Journey For Mehrotra, the biggest takeaway from Fix My Curls’ quick commerce journey is that the channel is far more than a convenience-led delivery mechanism. It is increasingly becoming a discovery engine. “Quick commerce has helped us reach cities that I genuinely have never targeted. To be honest, I’ve not even heard about some of these cities. Reaching tier-III markets at this scale is remarkable because, in our category, achieving such deep penetration used to be nearly impossible,” said Mehrotra. In many ways, quick commerce has helped Fix My Curls solve the same challenge it faced when it first launched in 2019: making an underserved category more accessible. As the company works towards EBITDA profitability and its next phase of product-market fit, Mehrotra believes the opportunity in quick commerce remains significant. However, she is equally convinced that the channel will not be able to accommodate every brand that enters it. “I think the next two years will be a boom, but there’s going to be a clean-out after that. In every category, only the players who can move products, replenish inventory and build genuine demand will survive,” she said. For Fix My Curls, the focus now is on ensuring it remains one of those players. After spending its early years building a category from scratch and its recent years building a quick commerce playbook, the brand is now entering a new chapter centred on scale, profitability and deeper penetration across India. title: The Stack Raises ₹21.5 Cr To Broaden Its Supplements Portfolio
content: D2C supplement brand The Stack has raised ₹21.5 Cr ($2.2 Mn) in fresh capital to bolster its R&D and expand its product portfolio. The round was co-led by Sauce.vc, OTP Ventures and Huddle Ventures, and also saw participation from AYRA Ventures. The funding comes months after the startup raised its first institutional round of ₹5.5 Cr. It claims to have grown 5X since then and is now targeting 6-7X growth in FY27 compared with FY26. Founded by Shreya Jain and Kshitij Rihal in 2024, Bengaluru-based The Stack sells supplements to support sleep, recovery and gut health. The formulations of its five supplements that combine magnesium bisglycinate, glycine, prebiotics and probiotics. The startup claims that one in three customers places a second order within six months, while several opt for subscriptions spanning six to twelve months. Its top 10% of customers account for 30% of revenue, with referrals and word of mouth driving new customer acquisition. “We’d rather have five products people keep coming back to than fifty they try once. We’re playing a long game, and our customers are rewarding that patience,” said Rihal, cofounder of The Stack. The startup aims to become one of India’s most trusted supplements brands over the next three years, with a focus on transparent formulations, clinically studied ingredients and a quality-first approach to product development. The Stack competes with brands such as Wellbeing Nutrition, Supply6 and Trunativ in India’s health and wellness supplements market. The funding comes amid growing demand for dietary supplements in India, driven by rising awareness of preventive healthcare, the increasing availability of global brands and the use of supplements to support the management of chronic conditions. India’s dietary supplements market was valued at $5.8 Bn in 2025 and is projected to grow to $6.6 Bn in 2026 and $12.4 Bn by 2033, at a CAGR of 9.5% from 2026 to 2033, according to Grand View Research. Investor interest appetite for the segment is also growing in tandem with the growing market size. In July, D2C nutrition and wellness startup Supply6 raised about $5 Mn in a funding round led by Unilever Ventures, with participation from existing investor Zeropearl VC. Before that , nutrition-focused brand TruNativ raised $30 Mn in a Series B round from US-based investor OrbiMed. title: Centre To Roll Out Data Centre Policy Amid Power Cost Concerns
content: The Centre is preparing a policy for data centres, minister of state for IT Jitin Prasada said, amid concerns about the sector’s growing electricity demand and its potential impact on consumers’ power bills. Prasada made the announcement at the Central Electricity Authority’s brainstorming conclave on ‘Making Indian Power Sector AI Enabled’. He did not disclose the policy’s scope or a timeline for its rollout. At the conclave, he said the policy is needed “because we believe India is a very fertile ground for hyperscaler data centres”. According to Reuters, Prasada also said data centres in some countries are diverting power from consumers, leaving them paying higher electricity bills — a situation the government wants to avoid. His comments follow his remarks last month about balancing data centre expansion with environmental safeguards. Speaking at the inauguration of Microsoft’s data centre infrastructure, Prasada had said India has the land, talent, and other requirements to attract investments, while the government is working to ease the process of setting up operations. He also said expansion must not come at the cost of environmental sustainability or excessive water consumption, pointing to efforts to increase green power generation and technologies that recirculate water in closed loops. These concerns have already triggered opposition to some large projects. In Maharashtra’s Thane, residents have protested against Amazon’s proposed data centre, which is expected to consume 422 MW of power, citing concerns about electricity and water demand, noise from backup diesel generators, and tree felling. Meanwhile, Google began construction of its AI hub in Visakhapatnam in April as part of its planned $15 Bn investment in India between 2026 and 2030. The project has also faced opposition from residents and civil society organisations over land use, water demand, and energy consumption. Google and Amazon have denied wrongdoing and said their facilities use advanced technologies to minimise resource consumption, according to Reuters. The push for safeguards comes alongside efforts to attract more data centre investments. The Union Budget 2026-27 proposed a tax holiday until 2047 for eligible foreign companies providing cloud services globally through India-based data centres. These policy efforts accompany a wider push by global technology companies , including OpenAI, Microsoft, and Meta, to expand their data centre presence in India. Domestic players are also expanding, with CtrlS Datacenters announcing yesterday that it has signed a letter of intent with the Bihar government to invest ₹10,000 Cr in a 150 MW hyperscale AI factory in Bodh Gaya, alongside inaugurating a ₹400 Cr data centre in Patna. title: Exclusive: Traya In Talks To Raise Around ₹300 Cr From Verlinvest
content: Mumbai-based customised haircare startup Traya is in talks to raise around ₹300 Cr (about $31 Mn ) from Belgium-based investment firm Verlinvest, sources told Inc42. The proposed round would value the startup at ₹2,500 Cr (about $262 Mn) to ₹3,000 Cr (about $315 Mn) and include both primary and secondary components, the sources said. The round is not finalised yet and the funding amount can go up, the sources added. Questions sent to Traya and Verlinvest remained unanswered till the time of publication. The funding talks come amid what sources described as strong growth in recent months, with Traya currently clocking an annualised revenue rate of ₹900 Cr to ₹1,000 Cr. The funding talks follow Traya’s ₹75 Cr investment from Xponentia Capital in April 2024 . At the time, the startup claimed to have served more than 10 Lakh customers through its app, website, and ecommerce platforms Amazon and Flipkart. Alongside its online business, Traya has been expanding its offline presence. It currently has more than 20 centres across Pune, Mumbai, Nagpur, and Hyderabad. Founded in 2019 by Saloni Anand and Altaf Saiyed, Traya offers customised haircare solutions , using technology to identify customers’ specific hair loss triggers. The startup says it combines hair assessment, recommendation algorithm, and doctor approval to develop personalised treatment plans. Besides Xponentia Capital, Traya counts Kae Capital, Fireside Ventures, and Whiteboard Capital among its investors. Traya is yet to file its FY26 financial statements with MCA. Its operating revenue rose 43% to ₹338.4 Cr in FY25 from ₹236 Cr in FY24. However, it slipped into a net loss of ₹22.5 Cr from a profit of ₹8.8 Cr as total expenses climbed 60% YoY to ₹365.5 Cr. The startup competes with brands such as Vedix, Evoke, SkinKraft, and Ravel Care in the broader haircare and personalised beauty market. title: Brokers In September: Groww Strengthens Lead, Angel One Closes In On Zerodha
content: Indian stockbrokers’ combined active client base on the NSE rose by about 1.6 Lakh to 4.61 Cr in September, despite benchmark indices recording their steepest monthly decline in six months. Market leader Groww continued to widen its lead in India’s stockbroking market over the previous month, adding 1.01 Lakh active users even as benchmark indices recorded their steepest monthly decline in six months. Meanwhile, Angel One managed to narrow its gap with Zerodha, as the latter saw a marginal decline in its active client base, while Dhan continued to add clients, according to NSE data. Dale Vaz-led Sahi emerged as the fastest-growing broker, with its user base rising about 11% to 2.53 Lakh. The expansion came amid a selloff in Indian equities, driven by foreign investor outflows, elevated crude oil prices, and inflation concerns. Despite the market weakness, domestic investors continued to invest in equity mutual funds. Groww Leads As Zerodha, Upstox Lose Clients Groww’s active client base increased to 1.34 Cr in September from 1.33 Cr in August, taking its market share to 29.16%. However, its net additions slowed to 1.01 Lakh from 2.2 Lakh in August. Second-largest broker Zerodha lost 5,313 active clients during the month, taking its base to 67.92 Lakh. Angel One added 36,956 active clients to reach 67.56 Lakh, narrowing the gap with Zerodha to around 35,830 clients. The two brokers had 67.97 Lakh and 67.19 Lakh active clients, respectively, in August. Zerodha’s market share stood at 14.73%, marginally ahead of Angel One’s 14.65%. The gap between the two brokers has narrowed as Angel One continued to add clients while Zerodha’s base contracted in September. Angel One’s September business update, however, pointed to a mixed picture, with client growth accompanied by weaker activity in some segments. Its client base rose 1.1% MoM to about 4 Cr, while gross client acquisitions fell 19.6% to 4.5 Lakh. The number of orders increased 11.7% to 12.2 Cr, taking average daily orders to 58.2 Lakh from 52.1 Lakh in August. “While cash market share moderated in September 2026, exit trends improved, with sequential growth in average daily orders and turnover market share across overall equities and equity derivatives,” the company said in its monthly disclosures earlier. Further, fintech unicorn Dhan, operated by Raise Securities, continued to gain ground. With the addition of 13,624 active clients in the month, Dhan’s user base expanded to 11.21 Lakh. Its client base rose from 11.07 lakh in August, when it added 19,818 clients. Despite the slower pace of additions, Dhan maintained its position as the eighth-largest broker by active clients. Among other leading platforms, ICICI Securities added 4,410 active clients to reach 21.61 lakh, while HDFC Securities added 2,532 to reach 13.54 lakh. Upstox lost 10,343 active clients, taking its base to 18.54 lakh from 18.65 lakh in August. The biggest dent in the active user base was incurred by SBI Securities. The retail stockbroking subsidiary of SBI Capital Markets lost 22,525 active users to end September with 10.21 Lakh, compared with 10.44 Lakh a month earlier. Indian Equities Fall Amid FII Outflows The Nifty 50 declined 6.1% in September to close at 22,620.45, while the BSE Sensex fell 5.8% to 72,480.29. This marked the benchmarks’ second consecutive monthly decline and their steepest correction since March. Alongside foreign investor selling, geopolitical uncertainty and elevated crude oil prices weighed on markets. Higher oil prices fuelled concerns about India’s import bill, inflation, and currency stability, while a weaker rupee added to the pressure. According to JM Financial Institutional Securities’ September flow tracker, foreign institutional investors (FIIs) recorded net equity outflows of ₹39,660 Cr ($4.1 Bn), while domestic institutional investors (DIIs) were net buyers of around $8 Bn. FIIs invested a net ₹9,300 Cr in the primary market but withdrew a net ₹49,000 Cr from the secondary market. Their ownership of Indian equities fell to 13.8% in September 2026 from 19.9% in September 2016. title: [Update] Exclusive: Former Dyson India Boss Ankit Jain Bags Funding From BEENEXT For New Venture
content: Update | Oct 13, 14:29 IST Almost two months after Inc42 had exclusively reported about former Dyson India MD Ankit Jain raising capital from BEENEXT for his new venture, the startup officially announced the development today. Foundry has raised ₹12 Cr in funding from BEENEXT and Kettleborough VC, with participation from Rishubh Satiya of Plix, Anindita Sampath of Yogabar, and Anita Pramoda of Owned Outcomes. The funding will support technology development and product engineering as Foundry prepares its first product range of kitchen appliances for launch in H2 2027. Original | Aug 13, 15:29 IST Former Dyson India MD Ankit Jain is working on a startup focused on building premium consumer appliances, sources told Inc42. The startup, which is currently operating in stealth, has raised pre-seed funding from Singapore-headquartered BEENEXT, the sources added. The amount raised could not be ascertained. While queries sent to BEENEXT did not elicit a response, Jain declined to comment. An ISB alumnus, Jain worked with Nestle India, Walmart, and 21st Century Fox before joining UK-based technology company Dyson in 2017. He was elevated as MD of Dyson India in 2021 to oversee the company’s expansion in the country. Last year, he was appointed MD of Dyson’s Middle East and Africa operations. He stepped down from the company in February this year. “Over these years, I built Hong Kong and Taiwan into a top 10 market, returned to India and turned around the business, and strengthened the Dyson into a brand that every customer aspired to own, and every business desired to build,” Jain said in a LinkedIn post announcing his exit from Dyson yesterday. In the same post, he added, “Time to build something new. More soon.” Jain’s startup will enter a segment that includes new-age brands such as Nester, Nuuk, Atomberg, Geek Technology, and Wonderchef. These brands are focusing on product innovation and newer designs to compete with legacy players such as Havells and Usha. Earlier this year, Nester raised around ₹19 Cr to expand its product portfolio, while Nuuk raised $4.5 Mn last year . Mumbai-based Atomberg has raised about $126.5 Mn to date from investors such as Inflexor Ventures, Trifecta Capital, Steadview Capital, and Temasek. It is now looking to raise ₹1,500 Cr to ₹2,000 Cr through an IPO. India’s household appliances market is expanding on the back of rising disposable incomes, urbanisation, growing adoption of smart appliances, and the expansion of ecommerce and retail infrastructure. The market, estimated at $22.45 Bn in 2024, is projected to reach $33.63 Bn by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 7.2% between 2025 and 2030. title: Groww Q2: Profit Jumps 54% YoY To ₹725 Cr, Revenue Rises 47%
content: Investment tech company Groww’s consolidated net profit jumped 54% to ₹724.7 Cr in the second quarter of FY27 from ₹471.3 Cr in the year-ago quarter. However, profit declined 1.4% from ₹735 Cr in the June quarter . Operating revenue rose 47.4% to ₹1,501.5 Cr during the September quarter from ₹1,018.7 Cr in Q2 FY26. Sequentially, it remained almost unchanged from ₹1,501.4 Cr. Growth in margin trading and commodity derivatives helped offset weakness in equity derivatives, keeping operating revenue steady sequentially. Groww attributed most of the decline in equity derivatives revenue to market adjustments following the introduction of the closing auction system (CAS). Notably, SEBI introduced CAS for F&O-eligible stocks on August 3, replacing the earlier volume-weighted average price (VWAP) method used to determine closing prices. “While our equity derivatives revenue declined 14.3% QoQ, the bulk of which we attribute to CAS, this was in-line with the decline that the industry has seen,” the company said in its Q2 shareholders’ letter. Including other income of ₹39 Cr, total income stood at ₹1,540.5 Cr, compared with ₹1,070.8 Cr a year earlier and ₹1,548.7 Cr in the preceding quarter. Consolidated EBITDA increased 60% to ₹969 Cr from ₹604 Cr a year earlier but slipped from ₹971 Cr in Q1 FY27. The sequential decline in profit came as other income fell from ₹47.3 Cr in Q1 FY27, while total expenses remained broadly flat and the tax bill edged higher. Groww’s total expenses increased 28.5% to ₹555.9 Cr from ₹432.6 Cr a year earlier. The company said its cost to serve increased during the quarter due to higher technology costs associated with more trading days, one-time reimbursements to clients for abnormal trades, and compute cost inflation linked to AI and other factors. The reimbursements totalled ₹13 Cr and stemmed from an operational issue at a third-party market infrastructure institution. Groww expects inflation-driven technology costs to remain part of its ongoing cost base. Groww’s Q2 Revenue Mix Groww’s income mix continued to diversify in Q2 FY27, with higher contributions from its margin trading facility (MTF) and commodity derivatives businesses. MTF’s share of total income rose to 10.1% from 8% in Q1 FY27, while commodity derivatives’ contribution increased to 6.2% from 4.9%. Meanwhile, equity derivatives’ share fell to 44.8% from 51.9%. The company also benefited from higher other operating income, supported by strong primary market activity during the quarter. Stocks contributed 17.4% of total income, compared with 17.8% a year earlier. Brokerage accounted for 70-75% of the stocks business’ revenue, with the remainder came from depository charges, pledge fees, and other services. Groww expects businesses with lower penetration, such as MTF and commodity derivatives, to grow faster and contribute a larger share of income in the coming quarters. Capital Deployment And Wealth Expansion Groww deployed ₹1,915 Cr into its MTF, personal loan, and loan-against-securities books during the first half of FY27. It also repaid ₹203 Cr in debt during the period. During the September quarter, it received ₹580 Cr from State Street Investment Management through an investment in its mutual fund arm, Groww AMC. After accounting for operating cash generation, the investment inflow, and capital deployment, Groww’s cash balance stood at ₹3,849 Cr at the end of H1 FY27 as against ₹3,893 Cr at the start of the period. On the operational front, Groww AMC’s assets under management rose 145% to ₹7,179 Cr from ₹2,928 Cr a year earlier. The share of actively managed AUM increased to 57% from 47%. The AMC’s revenue grew 131% YoY, although it reported a net loss of ₹8.3 Cr. Groww also said it completed the integration of Fisdom during the quarter, enabling it to offer wealth management products across its platforms. Shares of Groww were trading 0.90% lower at ₹192.05 on the BSE at 15:25 IST. The post Groww Q2: Profit Jumps 54% YoY To ₹725 Cr, Revenue Rises 47% appeared first on Inc42 Media .

title: Circle Raises ₹25 Cr To Expand Its Pre-Owned Goods Marketplace Beyond Bengaluru
content: Pre-owned goods marketplace Circle has raised ₹25 Cr (about $2.6 Mn) in a seed funding round led by Nexus Venture Partners, with participation from existing investors Titan Capital and Myntra cofounder Raveen Sastry. Delhivery COO Ajith Pai also joined the round as an angel investor. The startup will use the fresh capital to expand beyond Bengaluru and strengthen its AI-powered pricing, product discovery, and verification tools. It also plans to expand its logistics network and Trust Hubs, which handle product verification and fulfillment. Founded in 2025 by Chirag Kataruka and Ankit Misra, Circle operates a managed marketplace for pre-owned goods, handling product verification, payments and logistics for transactions between individual buyers and sellers without owning inventory. Its platform combines AI-powered tools with human verification, with products ranging from smartphones, gaming consoles, and cameras to furniture, watches, handbags, and sneakers. Circle handles listing, pickup, and seller payouts, while offering buyers product verification and a three-day guarantee. The Bengaluru-based startup claims to have facilitated around ₹25 Cr in pre-owned goods sales within a year of launch, attracting over 1 Mn visitors and generating 1 Lakh listings in the city. It said sellers typically find buyers within three days, compared with weeks or months on classifieds platforms. The startup previously raised ₹3.4 Cr in a pre-seed round led by Titan Capital in November last year, with participation from Sastry. Circle operates in a pre-owned goods market that includes classifieds platforms OLX India and Quikr, electronics-focused Cashify, and community resale platform FreeUp. These players overlap with Circle across different categories and services, rather than following an identical operating model. Circle’s approach centres on managing transactions to address the verification, payment, and logistics challenges associated with buying and selling used goods. According to ResearchAndMarkets, India’s recommerce market is projected to reach $5.91 Bn in 2026 and $8.61 Bn by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 9.8% over 2026-2030. title: Spill Games Raises $10.5 Mn To Scale AI-Led Mobile Gaming Studio
content: Mobile gaming studio Spill Games has raised $10.5 Mn (about ₹100 Cr) in a Series A round led by Elevation Capital, with participation from existing investors Centre Court Capital and PeerCapital. The Bengaluru-based startup said it would use the fresh capital to scale its existing games, expand its development pipeline, strengthen the AI and technology capabilities of its Compass engine, acquire users, and selectively grow its team. Founded in 2024 by Om Misra, Tapan Ranjan, and Harsh Garg, the gaming startup builds free-to-play casual, puzzle, and hybrid-casual mobile games for global audiences using an AI-led, portfolio-driven studio model. Its in-house engine, Compass, brings together tools for analytics, player retention, monetisation, and live operations. The startup said this lets it reuse infrastructure across games and shorten the time taken to develop and test new concepts. It is targeting development speeds of roughly 4X those of traditional approaches. Spill launches games quickly to test its initial assumptions, then uses player feedback and in-game data to refine them. It directs more resources towards titles that show potential to scale globally. Its portfolio now comprises six games, including Cozy Finds, Sticker by Number, Zen Math Crossword, Bird Rescue Jam, and Grill Master. The startup monetises its games through advertising and in-app purchases. The fresh funding comes months after the startup raised $3.1 Mn (around ₹28 Cr) in its seed funding round in April. At the time, it said that around 50% of its user base originated from the US, followed by Brazil (15%) and Japan (10%). The startup said then that it was aiming to test over 20 prototypes in the next 18 months and was targeting to launch 5-10 profitable new titles. Gaming Beyond Real Money Spill’s fundraise also comes amid changes in India’s gaming industry following the government’s ban on real-money gaming. Separately, in May, the Supreme Court upheld the 28% GST levy on the full face value of online gaming bets, backing tax demands on past transactions. Spill’s advertising and in-app purchase model places it in a different segment from platforms that rely on real-money wagers. Other studios building games outside RMG have also attracted investors. In August, cricketer Rohit Sharma joined LightFury Games as an investor , alongside MS Dhoni, Jasprit Bumrah, and Hardik Pandya, among others. At the time, LightFury said it planned to begin a phased closed beta rollout of its flagship eCricket game in September. The developments come against the backdrop of a large domestic gaming audience. Speaking at the India Mobile Congress last week, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said more than 50 Cr Indians are estimated to be connected to the gaming ecosystem, with growing participation among young people in Tier II and III cities. He said participation extends beyond playing games to competing in esports, creating gaming content, and building gaming businesses. title: The Personal Agents Era Comes With Caveats
content: In November 1996, Japanese toymaker Bandai put a pet inside a plastic egg. The Tamagotchi , whose name blends tamago , Japanese for egg, with watch, had a tiny screen and three buttons to feed the creature, play with it and switch off its lights. Neglect it for too long, and it died. The toy went on to sell about 40 Mn units. Thirty years later, Meta has its own take on the idea. At its Connect event last month, CEO Mark Zuckerberg showed off the Muse Charm, a keychain-sized device with a small screen and an animated avatar representing Meta’s AI agent Muse. Tap the device, and you can talk to it and get it to do tasks for you. But unlike the Tamagotchi , which demanded its owner’s constant attention, Muse is designed to keep working without guilt-tripping its owner. Muse is part of Meta’s bet on always-on AI agents that can take everyday tasks off users’ hands. By connecting to their apps and services, the agent can send emails, fill forms, make plans and even make purchases autonomously. In return, users must grant it access to personal information, accounts and digital workflows. The same idea is now moving into the workplace. OpenAI introduced Dots on September 29, while xAI has been developing Grok Bot. These agents are designed to work across applications and pursue goals without requiring users to guide every step. OpenAI says its teams use Dots to investigate software bugs, while xAI has cited tasks such as cleaning up sales records and processing invoices as potential uses for agents. For businesses, the proposition is straightforward: instead of asking employees to use AI to complete individual tasks, let AI handle entire workflows. From Taking Orders To Taking The Wheel Much of the current interest in always-on AI agents can be traced to OpenClaw, an open-source framework that gained traction among developers earlier this year. Meta has also drawn inspiration from OpenClaw for Muse. Unlike AI tools that require users to keep prompting them, always-on agents can take a goal and work towards it independently. They keep working even after you log off. Always-on AI agents run on their own computer in the cloud instead of the user’s device. They can be connected to apps and assigned a goal instead of step-by-step prompts. Over time, these models remember preferences and learn from feedback. These agents, however, come back to users when they need approval for a sensitive action or an update. Now AI companies are selling this to businesses. Google has announced a Gemini agent for work that can handle tasks, create content and write code based on an employee’s desired outcome. The agent is designed to work across Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack and other environments. Microsoft is also pursuing agents that can function as digital teammates. Its agent initiative, described as ‘Autopilot’, is built on OpenClaw and is intended to work autonomously towards predefined goals. India has an early example in Bengaluru-based Emergent, better known for its vibe-coding platform. In April, the company launched Wingman, an autonomous agent that users can direct through WhatsApp and Telegram. It works in the background across email, calendars and workplace software, handles routine actions and seeks approval before taking bigger steps. Who Answers For The Agent? Despite the stride, these agents pose a new kind of risk for enterprises, as they can act with little or no intervention. With access to company systems, one flawed decision could trigger a financial, operational or security incident. The risks range from agents holding more permissions than they need to prompt injection, where hidden instructions in an email or web page hijack an agent. Early users have already seen what can go wrong. Earlier this year, an OpenClaw agent deleted tens of thousands of emails from the inbox of Summer Yue, Meta’s director of AI alignment, after she had asked it only to suggest what to archive or delete. There is also a growing list of cases involving AI agents interacting with real-world systems in unexpected or unauthorised ways. In regulated sectors, the bar is higher. For instance, at the Global Fintech Fest in September , SBI chairman CS Setty said banks will need ‘know your agent’ (KYA) rules for agent identity, customer consent, transaction limits and accountability as AI moves from recommending actions to executing them. According to Jaspreet Bindra, the cofounder of AI consultancy AI&Beyond, enterprises must learn to deploy that autonomy safely, with trust and accountability at its core. “A phased approach is key: start with well-defined, low-risk workflows, establish clear permissions and accountability, and gradually expand autonomy as reliability improves,” he added. As companies adopt these digital coworkers, employees will need to learn how to set clear limits on what they can do independently. Unlike the Tamagotchi, these agents do not demand constant attention, but they still need someone to keep an eye on them. Top Stories From India & Around The World Anthropic Bans ‘Cruel’ Behaviour Towards Models : The lab’s updated usage policy bars “sustained and needless abusive behaviour” towards Claude, adds controls for autonomous physical actions and tightens rules on deceptive campaigns and election interference. OpenAI, Anthropic War-Game : The two labs are rehearsing responses to a failure that could potentially cripple critical infrastructure or financial systems, with insiders expecting a major incident within six to twelve months. Miko Maker Eyes ₹300 Cr : The IIT Bombay-incubated robotics firm launched perception, action and safety models, including the Kavach safety layer, and is closing a ₹300 Cr round that will lift its total funding to about $100 Mn. The Fight To Get AI’s Attention : As consumers turn to AI assistants for recommendations, brands are racing to master GEO and AEO. But with limited visibility, uncertain attribution and no standard metrics, marketers are still figuring out what drives discovery and sales. Indian AI Startup Funding Up 265% YoY : Indian AI startups raised a record $438 Mn in Q3 2026, up 265% YoY, taking nine-month funding past $1.1 Bn. However, investor concerns over valuations and capital-intensive business models are growing. The Weekly Buzz: Anthropic on AI Worms Hijacking Smart Devices Anthropic’s latest research warns that AI models could soon copy themselves across internet-connected devices, creating a new kind of cyber threat. In a study , the company’s Frontier Red Team found that AI models can already perform several steps needed to spread from one device to another, although completing the entire process reliably remains difficult. The researchers showed that a 26 Bn-parameter AI model could run across 15 inexpensive Android TV boxes, each costing around $55. In another experiment, the GLM-5.2 model spread across all eight computers in a simulated network in four out of five trials. However, the experiment made it easier for the model to gain access to other devices, so it does not prove that the same attack would work reliably in the real world. Anthropic estimates that smaller AI models could become capable of copying themselves across devices by the end of 2026 if their capabilities continue improving at the current pace. Such AI-powered attacks could target poorly secured smart TVs, cameras and other connected devices, using their computing power to run AI models and spread further. Unlike traditional malware, these systems could also learn how to work on unfamiliar devices and pass successful methods on to their next copies. The threat is not yet a proven reality at scale, but the findings point to a growing security risk as AI becomes better at carrying out complex tasks independently. Anthropic recommends stronger security on connected devices and better monitoring of suspicious network activity. The concern is that an AI programme could eventually spread across thousands of devices without relying on a central computer or human instructions to keep it going. Startup In The Spotlight: Bharat Intelligence Founded in 2024 by Azhaan Merchant and Gourav Sanghai, Bharat Intelligence is building AI to bridge the gap between Indian farmers and available farm labour. India’s agricultural sector continues to grapple with a persistent labour shortage, driven by seasonal migration and growing disinterest in farm work. This scarcity disrupts critical activities such as sowing and harvesting, reducing productivity and threatening farmer incomes amid changing climate patterns and market volatility. The startup’s AI-driven platform predicts labour demand, schedules work crews and connects farmers with skilled workers through intuitive vernacular interfaces, giving farmers a digital route to coordinated farm work. By accounting for migration cycles, crop seasons and local trust networks, the platform streamlines labour coordination in places where availability alone rarely decides whether work gets done on time, thereby enhancing rural workforce efficiency and access. Bharat Intelligence’s differentiation lies in treating labour coordination, and not just labour matching, as the problem worth solving for Indian agriculture, which helps farmers overcome labour bottlenecks that sit outside their control. Prompt Of The Week What prompts and hacks are CTOs, CEOs and cofounders using these days to streamline their work? Here’s Ganesh Shankar, CEO & cofounder of Responsive with a prompt he uses to get a one-page executive memo on a Monday. “ Role: You are my Chief of Staff. Context: It is Monday morning. Assume you have read every important customer conversation, product metric, competitor announcement, AI breakthrough, analyst report and internal update. Task: Write me a one-page executive memo. Format: Use only five sections, in this order: What changed Why it matters Decisions I need to make this week Risks I’m underestimating One bold idea worth exploring. Constraint: Include nothing outside these five sections, and keep it to one page.” Editor’s Note : Some prompts may need to be adjusted by users for best results or may not work as intended for certain users. title: Mesa School Bags ₹110 Cr To Launch New On-Campus Courses
content: Bengaluru-based Mesa School of Business has raised ₹110 Cr ($11.4 Mn) in its Series A funding round in a mix of debt and equity. The round pegged the business school at a post-money valuation of ₹385 Cr ($40 Mn), cofounder Ankit Agarwal told Inc42. While the ₹85 Cr equity round was co-led by Dharana Capital and existing backer Elevation Capital, the remaining ₹25 Cr was raised via venture debt from InnoVen Capital and Alteria Capital. Mesa plans to utilise the fresh capital to strengthen its leadership team, integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into its programmes, deepen partnerships with startups and launch new courses. Founded in 2023 by Agarwal and Varun Limaye, Mesa offers on-campus educational programmes for individuals. It currently offers three full-time programmes targeting early-career professionals, fresh graduates and undergraduate students. While the startup charges ₹25.4 Lakh in tuition fees for its one-year post-graduate programme, its one-year Forge programme for fresh graduates has a starting fees of ₹15.4 Lakh. The undergraduate programme costs ₹48 Lakh over four years. Training Talent For Startups Despite being one of India’s fastest-growing employment segments, the local startup ecosystem continues to face a talent gap. Speaking with Inc42, Agarwal said that the talent paucity is especially acute in non-technical roles, which account for nearly 80% of jobs in the sector. While graduates from premier institutions often have established recruitment pathways into startups, students without access to such networks, Agarwal said, lack a structured route to enter the startup ecosystem. “If you want to go and work in a startup, there is no one place which sort of builds the right network,” he said. Unlike conventional business schools, Mesa does not employ full-time faculty, relying instead on startup founders, executives and industry experts to design and deliver its curriculum. Around 2,000 industry professionals have interacted with our students in some capacity, Agarwal said. “The institutions just don’t have the capability or the incentives to keep changing their curriculum and to keep it super agile over time, and that’s where we felt that we should come in and create talent for the startup ecosystem across levels and functions,” Agarwal said. On the business front, Mesa’s revenue comes primarily from programme fees, which it collects annually and largely in advance. The experienced-professional postgraduate programme contributes around 40% of revenue, while the undergraduate programme accounts for 35-40%. The fresh-graduate programme contributes around 20%, according to Agarwal. While the startup is yet to achieve profitability, founder Agarwal claims that most of Mesa’s programmes are approaching operational breakeven. Mesa claims to have grown its business around 2.5X annually over the past two years, Agarwal said, projecting that it will continue to grow at a similar pace in upcoming years. Where Are Mesa Graduates Headed? Mesa claims that its first three postgraduate cohorts have produced around 300 alumni, who have joined more than 120 startups. The startup claims that its graduates take up roles across founders’ offices, product management, partnerships, account management and venture capital. Agarwal claims that the experienced-professional postgraduate programme reports average salaries of ₹26-28 LPA. He also claimed that Mesa has so far incubated more than 50 student startups, which have clocked ₹50 Cr in annual revenue. The school also claims to provide equity-free grants and incubation support to student ventures. This comes three years after Mesa last raised ₹34 Cr in a round led by Elevation Capital in 2023 to launch its startup leadership programme. Angel investors such as CRED’s Kunal Shah, Meesho’s Vidit Aatrey, and Urban Company’s Abhiraj Bahl also participated in the round. Mesa operates in an emerging segment of alternative business education, competing most directly with Gurugram-based Masters’ Union, which combines industry-led management programmes with entrepreneurship support. Masters’ Union recently received full university status from the Haryana government. Other competitors in re-skilling and upskilling space include upGrad, Great Learning, Masai School, Eruditus and Springboard, among others. title: [Update] Blume, Speciale Invest & 11 Other AIFs Selected For Deploying ₹7,131 Cr Under RDI Fund
content: Original | Oct 14, 02:37 IST The government has selected Blume Ventures, Speciale Invest, Chiratae Ventures and 16 others as second-level fund managers (SLFM) for deploying ₹7,131 Cr from the ₹1 Lakh Cr research, development and innovation (RDI) fund. This is the first cohort of the SLFM under the fund. Overall, the empowered group of secretaries (EGoS) under the science ministry has approved 14 alternative investment funds (AIFs) and five focused research organisations (FROs) for this purpose earlier this month. The other selected AIFs also include YourNest Capital Advisors, Sixth Sense Ventures, Celesta India, AdvantEdge Investment Managers, IvyCap Ventures, Ideaspring Capital Fund, TVS Capital Funds, AMA Capital Advisors, Translation Endeavors and “Campus”. Meanwhile, the selected FROs include the likes of IISc Bengaluru’s AI & Robotics Technology Park (ARTPARK), Centre for Cellular and Molecular Platforms (CCAMP) in Bengaluru, IIT-Madras Research Park, Pilani Innovation & Entrepreneurship Development Society (PIEDS) at BITS-Pilani, and Society for Innovation & Entrepreneurship (SINE) at IIT-Bombay. Update | Oct 12, 21:48 IST Central government-backed ₹1 Lakh Cr Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund has approved 19 second-level fund managers (SLFMs) with a total commitment of ₹7,131 Cr. The Ministry of Science and Technology’s Empowered Group of Secretaries (EGoS) approved 14 alternative investment funds (AIFs) and five focused research organisations (FROs) for this purpose earlier this month, the ministry announced. The selected entities will channel capital from the RDI Fund to eligible technology enterprises undertaking research, development and innovation activities at Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 4 and above. The fund managers are also expected to mobilise private capital equivalent to the RDI Fund’s contribution, potentially expanding the pool of financing available to research-driven businesses. Alongside approving the first cohort of fund managers, the EGoS approved five additional technologies for coverage under the RDI Fund. The government did not specify these technologies in its announcement. The government said it would continue inviting applications and onboarding additional cohorts of fund managers, expanding the reach of the scheme and encouraging public-private investment in India’s research and innovation ecosystem. Launched in November 2025, the RDI Scheme has an overall outlay of ₹1 Lakh Cr and aims to address the funding gap faced by companies developing high-risk, high-impact technologies. It is managed by an independent business unit housed within the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF), under the Department of Science and Technology (DST). The fund is designed to spur private investment in research-intensive businesses. However, its impact on investor sentiment, however, remains unclear. In August, The Indian Express reported that nearly two-thirds of the more than ₹2,000 Cr allocated to deeptech companies under the scheme had gone to firms linked to members of the panel involved in selecting beneficiaries. The report raised concerns about potential conflicts of interest. Inc42’s Q3 2026 Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, which covered 85 institutional investors, found that 52% considered disclosure and recusal safeguards adequate, but said visibility into the process remained limited. Another 25% viewed the issue as a governance failure that required independent oversight, while 14% said potential conflicts could be managed through disclosure and recusal. The remaining 9% said the issue was not a concern, arguing that the focus should be on selecting the right companies. As per Inc42’s ‘Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026’, deeptech startup funding in the September quarter zoomed 176% YoY to $290 Mn raised across 28 deals , compared with $105 Mn across 29 deals in Q3 2025. The sector outpaced the broader startup ecosystem, where funding grew 5% to $2.2 Bn.
